Mr. Speaker, November 19 to 25 is Drug Awareness Week. To this end the Government of Prince Edward Island is working with schools, churches and other community organizations to promote the theme "Keep your dreams alive".
Through the media, classroom presentations, church bulletins and even through a one-act play people in my province are discussing a problem that affects many of its citizens.
We are all aware of the effects that alcohol and drug abuse have on the user, the user's family and the community as a whole. I hope and expect that the sincere and determined efforts being made in my province this week will increase the awareness of the dangers of drug abuse and contribute to an improved quality of life for all Islanders.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this is Colleges Week, 1989, I invite all my colleagues in the House to join me in paying tribute to those who work in college education, throughout Canada.
Courses given at the college level prepare our youth for university education and help them better choose the field of studies and the career that interest them.
CEGEPs and other college-level institutions also train our skilled labour, an essential element of our country's human resources.
Across Canada, more and more adults are registered for college courses. Colleges therefore play a key role in continuing education, especially in labour force retraining and the ongoing adjustment of workers to new technologies.
In short, colleges and vocational training institutes are an essential link in our education systems and a vital asset for a strong and dynamic economy.

Mr. Speaker, it is not that frequent that we in Canada can proudly announce world champions. It is even less frequent that I can do it for the Cariboo-Chilcotin.
Today, it gives me great pleasure to announce that the Canadian arm wrestling team consisting of both men and women have returned victorious with the over-all title from the world arm wrestling championships in Athens, Greece.
Hear, hear!

It gives me even greater pleasure to announce that for the second year in a row Mike Kadar, a resident of Nimpo Lake in my constituency, has been crowned world champion in the heavyweight class. Last year, Mr. Kadar proved he had the world's strongest right arm when he went undefeated in the world championships in Sweden. This year, in competition with the world's most powerful men, he reconfirmed his supremacy.
Arm wrestling is not a fancy or expensive sport. It has, however, ancient roots and world-wide popularity. I think the residents of Nimpo Lake as well as all of Canada should be proud of Mr. Mike Kadar.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The only thing I can add to that is that I know Nimpo Lake very well.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure I speak for all members of the House when I express relief that Karen Ridd from Winnipeg, someone who is working in El Salvador with Peace Brigades International, was released yesterday by the Treasury Police who had taken her into custody.
True to the spirit of the work of Peace Brigades International, e noticed that Karen refused to be released unless the Colombian woman who had been arrested with her was also released.
The work of people like Karen and Peace Brigades International, people who go to Central America to provide an escort service which is designed to protect Salvadorans who may be under threat of death or kidnapping, is truly in the spirit of Canada's peacekeeping role. These are people who are real peacekeepers, who put themselves, their bodies, between the victimized and the oppressors, in this case the Cristianni government.
I think it is about time the Canadian Government showed the courage of some of its citizens like Karen Ridd in El Salvador and put itself, diplomatically, politically and economically between the United States, its puppet regime in El Salvador, and the people of El Salvador.

Mr. Speaker, today I wish to pay a final tribute to our colleague and friend, Jean-Claude Malepart, whose death is a grievous loss for us all.
An outstanding Member of Parliament, Jean-Claude Malepart not only made his mark on Canadian politics but also left us with memories of a sensitive, fiery and determined man. With his sense of duty and justice and his courage to fight to the end for the causes he cared about for the good of his fellow citizens, he leaves an example of a model parliamentarian for all those who seek to excel.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to respectfully salute Jean-Claude, who lives on in my heart, with admiration and affection. Thank you, Jean-Claude!

Mr. Speaker, while the death squads continue to roam the streets of El Salvador with the blessing of the right wing military government, Canada continues to deport people to that country. In effect, this government is upholding the U.S. policy of aggression in El Salvador. Thirteen El Salvadorans have been removed from Canada since January 1.
I call on the government to stop immediately this removal of Salvadoran citizens from Canada, to increase our embassy staff in that region, to speed up the processing of family class and other visas for those who wish to leave, and to use minister's permits to bring people out who are in danger of their lives, perhaps because their husbands or spouses are here in Canada as refugee claimants.
I call on the Minister of Employment and Immigration to use every effort she can to bring the endangered people out of El Salvador and not to send people back to El Salvador.

Mr. Speaker, a strike by 2,200 crew members on federal government ships started in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia on November 11.
These union members work for the Coast Guard, Fisheries and Oceans, Public Works and National Defence. They have been without a contract for two years.
Treasury Board has been dragging its feet in negotiations, and now talks are not even taking place. There are a number of issues involved in this strike, but the most appalling is the wage disparity between east coast crews and west coast crews.
The federal government is supposed to have a policy of equal pay for equal work. RCMP and the Armed Forces are paid equally across the country according to rank. However, in this case, east coast workers receive an average of $2,500 less per year than their west coast counterparts. This is blatant discrimination against At-
November 21, 1989

Oral Questions
lantic Canadian workers. These people are being penalized financially for working on the east coast.
In addition, foreign fishing is rampant, the lobster season is opening in South West Nova without any patrols for enforcement, navigational aids are not being set, and if a freeze-up occurs many harbours will not be able to operate.
When will this government assume its responsibilities, give these eastern workers a fair settlement, and stop its policy of discriminating against Atlantic Canada?

Mr. Speaker, today, thousands of farm producers from Quebec and the rest of Canada travelled many miles and bravely withstood the cold to express their concerns about the future of agriculture in this country.
I will be out there with them, demonstrating in the presence of a number of Quebec Members.
They want a clear commitment from their federal representatives that we will stand firm during multilateral talks, especially at the next GATT round.
I have made an unqualified commitment, Mr. Speaker, in this respect.
Quebec producers demand adequate representation of Quebec on all Canadian teams at the multilateral talks. I could not agree more.
Today, on the anniversary of the day this Government was elected a second time, we must ensure that everything we do always reflects what we said in our election speeches and with our public commitments, and that is why, Mr. Speaker, I have made a solemn commitment, and I know the Quebec Caucus is solidly behind me.

Mr. Speaker, for a number of weeks now I have received calls and correspondence from a number of health care professionals who are really concerned about the goods and services tax and the impact it will have upon health care services in Canada.
For example, with respect to psychologists and their psychological services, they provide not only needed therapeutic services but useful and essential preventive health care. They are also a very cost-effective alternative to over-burdened psychiatric services. I am really concerned, as are they, that the imposition of the goods and services tax will affect our health services negatively.
There are also others, such as occupational therapists, who are in the same boat.

Mr. Speaker, in addition to this tax there are also the billions of dollars cut as a result of reduced transfer payments to the provinces, which will have a negative impact on health services in this country.

There was an error made by the local officer in Hull not to investigate to determine that the land and building was home for a strip joint. There was an error made in the headquarters in approving the loan. Procedures are being looked at to remedy this situation to ensure that does not happen again.

November 21, 1989

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)

decision in Montreal last November or October, I am not sure when, but in any event, he would make enquiries. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. Today, thousands and thousands of farmers from the UPA in Quebec and the OFA in Ontario are marching on Parliament Hill to protest the government's agricultural policy. They feel that they have been sold out in the free trade deal because their marketing boards have not been protected from imports. They feel that they were sold out because their incomes were capped at the GATT decision last spring. They feel that the government promised them open access to the U.S. market and they got a countervail on hogs.
I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture when is the government going to start keeping the promises it made a year ago today in the last election and stop selling out Canadian farmers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, other members of the House and I are always concerned about the welfare of agriculture. No one is more concerned than the members on this side
Oral Questions
of the House in the government and we have certainly demonstrated that.
The plain fact of the matter is that the hon. member is wrong on all three counts. He says the marketing boards have been undermined and dismantled and he is wrong in that regard. They have been protected under the Free Trade Agreement and they are being protected under the Free Trade Agreement. He says that we capped the incomes. That is wrong again, because as he knows the industrial price of milk rose by 39 cents per hectoliter. The hon. member says that we do not have market access to the United States. He is wrong again, because many, many agri-food industries are penetrating that market, are doing veiy well, are creating jobs in Canada and providing security to the agriculture community here in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, if the minister is all right and the farmers are all wrong, why are 12,000 of them marching on Parliament Hill today?
These thousands of farmers are concerned that the government is going to sell them out at the GATT council meeting on December 4 in Geneva, just as they were sold out in the free trade deal and with the capping of industrial milk. I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Agriculture what assurance he can give these 12,000 farmers marching on Parliament Hill today that they will not be sold out in the GATT council meeting, and that the government will not accept the ruling of the GATT panel to allow a flow of cheap surplus dairy commodities into Canada from the U.S. What assurance can the minister give, in view of the fact that our chief partners, the Cairns Group and the United States, are both opposing our position with regard to marketing boards and with regard to import controls on dairy products?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one of the reasons that there is concern within the agricultural community is that of the fear and the anxiety that is being perpetrated by people like the hon. member and other critics.
They are all wrong and you are all right?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fact is that the position of the federal government taken by the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister for International Trade

November 21, 1989
Oral Questions
at the MTN negotiations is to strengthen and to clarify Article 11 so that we will not have the kind of decision that was brought down by GATT with respect to ice cream and yogurt.
That has been the position of the government for a long time, notwithstanding the fact that members opposite were suggesting that we should not tamper with Article 11. We are tampering with it to strengthen and clarify it so that it will preserve the supply managed underpinnings upon which the supply managed systems and the import controls obtain their power.
This government has provided unprecedented support to the agricultural industry. In the grain and oilseed sector alone, between the years 1984-85 and 1988-89, a total of $11,777 billion has been allocated in support of that sector.
Furthermore, in 1984-85, the support for the Canadian agri-food industry was something in the order of $4.6 billion. In 1987-88, that exceeded $8 billion, 75 per cent of which was provided for by the federal government. That is the kind of support this government is giving and that is the kind of support it will continue to give.
Hear, hear!
Twelve thousand farmers are wrong and you're right?

The way Canada is trading away the future of our agriculture in
the GATT negotiations in Geneva is unacceptable-

On the other hand, for years, you did not want to
November 21, 1989

respond to Canadian dairy farmers, you never wanted to defend them. We were the first government to do so, Mr. Speaker. We have nothing to learn from those people about defending Canadian farmers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also have a question for the Solicitor General.
The minister now knows that the Commissioner of the RCMP before a committee this morning said that the superintendent of the Montreal region for the RCMP delayed issuing search warrants in the Grise case "because of the election". He said that in the committee this morning.
The member for Burnaby, earlier on November 7, asked the minister questions about the delay at that time. The minister, instead of saying he would look into it, came back with, to put it bluntly, his usual bluster and went on to attack the member who asked the question and said: "The commissioner is not just anyone. He is in charge of RCMP operations", et cetera, instead of pursuing the matter at hand.
Considering that this issue was raised November 7-indeed we raised this issue last May-and that the Commissioner of the RCMP admitted today there was a delay because of the election, why did the minister not do his job a week ago, a month ago, last spring, instead of just finding out this morning what was being said about this issue?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taken aback by the import of my colleague's query. Should I question the integrity of the Commissioner of the RCMP every time he makes a statement?
I had no reason to doubt the word of the commissioner. As I recall, last June the commissioner answered questions before the committee, and this morning he told the same committee that he had been mistaken and that he would make inquiries to find out why the decision was delayed.
I would suggest we can rely on the integrity of the Commissioner of the RCMP. He was very frank and honest, I did not have any reason to doubt his word, and I
Oral Questions
have no intention of asking for an inquiry every time an RCMP officer makes a statement.
I think we should let the RCMP shed light on this matter, as it has done and as it knows how to do. Mr. Speaker, it is very important to this House and to all Canadians that no questions be raised concerning the integrity of the RCMP and the commissioner.

Mr. Speaker, I say to the minister that it is his responsibility as Solicitor General of Canada to ensure that the RCMP is doing its job. He cannot pass the buck. The buck stops with the minister and he knows that. Considering that it was Mr. Inkster, not someone on this side of the House, who said in committee this morning that the course of action that ultimately led to a conviction was not taken "because of the election", will the minister now do his job and immediately find out why there was a delay and why there was hesitancy to prosecute, to look at evidence to see if court proceedings should be taken? Was it for political reasons or not? Is the minister now prepared to exercise his responsibility, or does he just want this thing to be buried? That is no way to conduct his responsibilities, and the minister knows it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat surprised at the question, but since I was quoted, I suggest we go back to what I said on November 7 this year, and I will quote exactly what I said:

"The RCMP is an honourable police force that acts without political interference. I would like to refer to what the RCMP Commissioner said himself in June before a committee of this House. He was very emphatic about this, and I believe that in order to protect the integrity of this police force we must let them do their job and conduct their investigation as they see fit with the utmost integrity".
He changed that testimony this morning.

Debate. The Hon. Minister of State for Employment and Immigration and Minister of State for Seniors (Mrs. Vezina).

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, fellow members of the House of Commons, I intend to treat the debate on Bill C-43 with all the seriousness it deserves, all the attention, the good will,
November 21, 1989

even unselfishness that various individuals and groups in my riding have for this great social issue.
For example, last Friday, my riding office received a petition with 10,000 names. It contained the names of
10,000	people in Rimouski and Temiscouata who said: "We are against abortion in any form for a normal pregnancy, that is one with no risk, and we are against it from the moment of conception."
Others representing a completely different school of thought told me quite clearly that only the woman concerned should decide whether or not to interrupt her pregnancy. One of them told me clearly that she never regretted having interrupted an unwanted pregnancy when she was 20.
I received the testimony of a father who said that he supports our bill, but who told his 13-year-old daughter who asked him what he would do if she came home pregnant: "If you wanted to terminate this pregnancy, we would take the necessary action. If you wanted to keep the child, we would want you to have a normal happy life and we would help you bring up this child as if it were our own."
Mr. Speaker, with these examples, I just want to show the interest all of society has in this most serious issue and the many points of view that we must consider as legislators, our main duty as elected representatives.
As far as I am concerned, I wish to state at the outset that I would certainly prefer to be somewhere else and not to have to participate in such a poignant, troubling discussion.
No one will say that abortion is an easy issue. No one will say that we can debate it light-heartedly, for the simple reason that no bill can ever faithfully reflect all shades of individual opinion on this agonizing question. In this regard, this House reflects Canadian society and the right to freedom of conscience which is one of its values.
No age or social group can escape the dilemma now facing society.
The decision to give birth is one of the most important, personal and private choices that can be made by a human being. But personal rights, health and life protection are also fundamental values that concern society as a whole. The balance we, as legislators, must maintain between a woman's right to choose whether or not to
Government Orders
interrupt her pregnancy and the state's responsibility to protect the foetus is extremely hard to find. Whether from a religious, moral, social, legal, medical or political standpoint, our conscience must inevitably grapple with this issue.
Mr. Speaker, over the last few months, like every other member of this House, I have been concerned with the abortion debate mobilizing Canadian men and women. I felt all the more concerned since I knew that a moment like today would come when, after thinking about it as parliamentarians, we would have to give this country a bill addressing the issue. Today I would like to share with you the various thoughts that come to my mind.
First, I would like to deal with our responsibility as legislators. I think it is important to properly define the realities we are talking about. At the risk of shocking some of my colleagues, I would suggest that the worst threat to the proceedings of this House would be to become idealistic. Finally, I would like to speak to the bill introduced by the government.
Mr. Speaker, I will deal first with our work as legislators. I want to stress how the debate that has just started is personally demanding. Seldom will our work be so challenging and require so much self-denial on the part of honorable members.
There is something extremely personal about the abortion issue. It challenges our most basic values and most private experiences. Yet, today I wish to emphasize the need for all of us, each and every one to somewhat distance ourselves from our own personal experience and opinions.
On this issue, the Right Hon. Prime Minister insisted on a free vote. He deserves to be praised for respecting our freedom of conscience. I appreciate the respect he is showing to Parliamentarians. But I see also in the Prime Minister's decision an invitation to reach out to others.
This new debate has nothing to do with what we personally think about the abortion issue. What is involved here is not what we would do in our heart of heart if we had to decide whether or not to terminate a pregnancy. No matter how free we are as members of the House, our debate must deal with the legislation which, as legislators, we must develop in Canada in the area of abortion.

Government Orders
Although I would not wish to show disrespect to any member of this House, I know that most Canadians men and women are not interested in our moods. They want us, as their elected representatives, to do our job.
Having sat in this House for nearly five years now, I trust that most of my colleagues will share my views. Mr. Speaker, I do not take part in this debate so much as Monique Vezina, the mother of four children, as the Hon. Member for the Rimouski-Temiscouata riding, duly elected by her constituents to provide our country with the legislation it needs.
Now to come to my second point. As a rule, I have always felt that, both as Parliamentarians and legislators, we had to show idealism, look toward a better world and strive to achieve it.
Today, however, in view of the very nature of the problem we are dealing with, I wish to state emphatically, without renouncing these ideals, that the principle of reality must prevail completely and totally in this forthcoming debate.
In 1988, there were between 73,000 and 74,000 therapeutic abortions in Canada. When reviewing the available data for previous years, it will be found the number has remained relatively unchanged. From 70,000 in 1982, it fell to some 65,000 in 1983-86. I conclude from those figures that abortion is a fact of life in Canada, a reality in our society. I also conclude that the women involved in those 74,000 therapeutic abortions wanted people to respect their personal decision. None of them claimed to have taken that course of action without some reluctance. They submit however that in all conscience that was the solution they chose.
Mr. Speaker, each and everyone in this House is hoping for that ideal world in which all those women could have all the financial means and the psychological and emotional strenght that would have let them bring their pregnancies to completion.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I am refering to the real world. Without sacrificing our dreams and our hopes, we must face up to the realities of human life where there will always be tragedies, where society will always be perfectible. I am asking that we as legislators recognize social reality in this country and the experience of Canadian women.
Let me turn to a third aspect, Bill C-43 as such. This government's challenge was to develop legislation that would fit with the Canadian reality. Yes, we looked for the area of widest possible social consensus. In any other area, we might be accused of being political opportunists. But in this matter this is the only tenable position.
What about the proposal? The Government states in the first place that abortion is a crime, and in the second place that it is not where it is induced in consultation with a who is of the opinion that if the abortion were not induced, the health or life of the female person would be likely to be threatened. There again, I suggest that we get away from any philosophical debate.
Personally, and along with large number of a very Canadian women, I also would have preferred that the legislation do not re-criminalize abortion. As legislator, I have found this to be impractical. This enactment is the only possible way to allow Parliament to regulate abortion nationally.
The legislation's first goal is not in my view to re-criminalize abortion nor, as claimed in some quarters, to return to situations where the lives of human beings, individuals, women are jeopardized in conditions that are worse than before.
Our first objective, therefore, under the circumstances, in the present Canadian context, is to take another step forward, another step to the future, taking account of our evolution as a society over the centuries, another step towards the equality of men and women: an equality which can only enrich both sexes with their complementarity, another step towards the fundamental freedom that we all seek. More and more men understand-and I know several among my colleagues who do-that subordination is not liberating for a couple, it is not liberating for a family, it is simply not liberating for the whole of a democratic country like ours. The same goes for our abortion bill.
Nevertheless, our government must be cautious and moderate, it must avoid venturing into uncharted waters, when many Canadians are telling us that we do not know how deep they are. The Government is instead choosing to bridge the two sides, the two extremes, so as to serve the most Canadians who want to use it. This bridge is our new legislation.

You will agree that we are taking a step forward, after the legal vacuum left by the Supreme Court judgment, when our government is eliminating the anomalies of the old law such as life imprisonment for women, among others. Also, as the Leader of the Opposition explained it so well in this House, we will no longer say that abortion is allowed if the mother's health is in danger, but if the mother's health is threatened.
Mr. Speaker, as a woman elected to this House, as a woman who has fought for recognition of women's rights, I urge all women who are still hesitant to cross this legislative bridge. I urge them to look back to the past, to look at history and remember how women have contributed to the development of this society. But they did so only when they could express themselves freely, as equals.
It is my profound belief that women must never give up their equality and their freedom. They should take advantage of this opportunity to perfect this very fundamental legislation and jump at the chance to increase their independence by having more control over their own bodies. That is what the new legislation will give them.
Men will also benefit because they will have friends, advisers, wives and doctors who are increasingly free, responsible and worthy of their trust.
There are critics in some groups who object that despite this national standard, there will be differences in treatment from one region to another, from one province to another. That is true, Mr. Speaker. However, I belong to a political party that has never been ashamed to recognize regional realities. As far as abortion is concerned, it is only natural that eveiy region in Canada should be able to proceed at its own pace. On what basis do they want to reduce Canada to a one-dimensional society? Here again, the government has made a genuine sociological reading of the abortion phenomenon and has drawn the appropriate conclusions.
Mr. Speaker, I do not claim that Bill C-43 is perfect. Far from it. I do say, however, that the greatness of our Canadian society and its ability to be a pluralistic society will be reflected in the ability of this House to vote.
These legal concerns will never reflect all the nuances that our hearts and minds want to express.
Government Orders
Mr. Speaker, we must therefore rise above that which might divide us irreparably and seek a common ground that is acceptable to the majority. Our most dependable guide posts in this respect are tolerance, understanding and maturity.
Mr. Speaker, we all realize that men and women benefit by change, even if change comes very gradually. That is why, speaking in this public and democratic forum, I urge women to support this bill, and I urge men to realize that when women change, so do they.
Together, let us cross the bridge the government has built for us. As a woman and a Member of Parliament, I say that we are going in the right direction.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with respect to the Hon. Secretary of State's speech. The tone of her speech had a great deal of dignity and I appreciate that. I appreciate also the difficulty with which she has explored her soul in this whole discussion about this very difficult question. I think she has set a tone tonight that is worthy of respect and I credit her for that.
I too have spoken with many people of different views in my own riding and I respect their views. However, when it comes to the responsibility of legislators, she and I have to part company. She said that we must give a bill to this House. I see no reason to give a bill to this House. I think it is only increasing the kind of pain that exists in our country now. This very debate is increasing that pain and encouraging the kind of lobby that is going on outside the House of Commons which is also increasing that pain.
We all dream of our ideal world, as the minister has said. My question to the hon. member really relates to the reasoning behind this bill. The minister said it was the only vehicle which would set down regulations on a national scale. The Criminal Code is not going to ensure access to abortion in the regions of our country where poor women are the ones who are having to turn to back street abortionists or having to terminate their pregnancies themselves.
How is Bill C-43 going to solve those problems?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Once again, Madam Speaker, I will refer to the principle of reality. When I look at the statistics as a woman and as a legislator I can readily see that last year 65,000 women had to undergo an abortion for whatever reason. There is a legal void. It is up to the provinces to guarantee access to health care, and as a woman and as a legislator I want to make sure that any woman seeking abortion services can do so with dignity, if I may put it that way, because it will be recognized as a medical act performed by a qualified medical practitioner in a recognized institution.
I used to be involved in development motivation. I met women and teenage girls. I saw how abortions were carried out in many cases. I deplore the fact that the legislative measure we are proposing involves the Criminal Code, but as we said on so many occasions, this is the only way to proceed at the national level if we want to enable Canadian women in any province to use this emergency service, this emergency measure, but with a medical approach, through a medical act which will take into account the quality of life.
That being so-the principle of reality-we must build a bridge which will reach both pro-life and pro-choice advocates, but within the context of Canadian reality. As legislators we must also implement measures to achieve this ideal project which will make it possible for women to protect the unborn child, practice family planning, and provide information.
And I maintain that with respect to this legislative measure, as a legislator I will support the government position because it enables us as a group of men and women to take a small step ahead, yet I would urge all women to continue to enjoy their freedom.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. minister a question, again with appreciation of the great thought that she has obviously given to this issue.
Given the minister's statement about the importance of women having access to good and proper medical care, can she explain to me why the bill in its present form provides an equal penalty for the totally unqualified person who preys on vulnerable women and provides abortions without any training to do so and for a
doctor exercising his best medical judgment who, for one reason or another, does not perhaps completely meet the intentions or the wording of the law?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
The answer that comes readily to mind is that I have faith in the medical profession. Our government considers abortion as a medical act that must be performed by a qualified physician. Doctors are men and women who also live by a professional code of ethics. Health will be defined by the medical body, which reassures me, as a woman, that women's health will be kept safe and private, since the woman will see a doctor with whom she will share responsibility for the decision. Having said that, I call on women, with whom I have worked for many years, to demand their right to quality services.
But the bill under consideration gives me the assurance that Canadian women throughout the country will be respected whatever the habits and customs of their province, because indeed habits vary from one province to the next, but that the decision to perform the medical act will be made with a clear conscience with the physician in appropriate quality surroundings. We are taking a step towards the acknowledgement of the freedom of the woman, of her sense of responsibility, of the right of the foetus. As a society we must acknowledge that women should have freedom as well as responsibilities-for responsibilities come with freedom-but we must also acknowledge the evolution of life. I would suggest that the bill enables us to reach both objectives.

Madam Speaker, I also appreciate the tone with which the minister speaks. I too am a social worker. I have practised in the field and have seen women die from illegal abortions.
I think women make the decision to terminate a pregnancy after a great deal of deliberation. They do so based on sound judgment, a knowledge of their own circumstances, and in consultation with their doctors.
For nearly two years now in Canada, we have had no criminal law on abortion. I think the women of Canada have demonstrated that they have acted responsibly during this time. They have shown Canadians that there is no need for any legislation, particularly criminal legislation, concerning abortion.
November 21, 1989

Government Orders
Is the minister aware of some particular circumstances in the last two years that would prompt her to feel that this House is more capable or more able to make a judgment than the woman herself in consultation with her doctor?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext: I repeat that the central government has to make sure that health care is of first quality and readily accessible to all Canadian men and women. This is why we must have this legal measure in place. Personally, as a legislator, I would rather not go through the kind of situation we were in last July. It is imperative that every Canadian woman-wherever she resides, I repeat-be entitled to that service. There exists a legal void which needs to be filled. This is a medical act which has to be recognized as such and performed by a physician. As a legislator I am convinced that the bridge we are proposing under this measure will enable the proponents of both positions to reach a common ground. As legislators we have to rise above personal opinions. What our constituents and Canadians expect of us as law makers in this House is that we take measures to improve the quality of life in this country, and such is the aim of our efforts: a medical approach, and proper balance between the right of the woman and the concern of society with respect to the evolution of the foetus and of human life.

Madam Speaker, the issue of abortion is a highly charged one for the House and for each of us as individual Members of Parliament, and also for the nation. It is even more so for the woman who finds herself pregnant unexpectedly and faces a situation in which carrying, bearing and raising a child seems an overwhelming impossibility. For her, the choice she faces is agonizing and painful.
For us as legislators, I believe the task is not to determine how, through law, we can impose our own individual consciences on all Canadian women. Rather, it is how we can draft a law that respects the right of a woman to exercise her conscience, that respects the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and its guarantees of the right to life and security of her person, but that also reflects the value society gives to the worth and dignity of human life.
Madam Speaker, whatever our opinion on abortion, the law must apply equally to all Canadians, rich or poor. It is not enough to say, as the Minister of Justice did two weeks ago, that it is a provincial decision as to what medical services are to be provided in their jurisdiction.

If I could return to the question of balance, we do not find this balance of rights and of interest in human life in most of the representations we have been receiving by the thousands. Instead we find two opposing views so strongly held as a matter of conscience that any meeting of the minds seems impossible. On the one hand are those who firmly believe in the existence of human life from the moment of conception and believe that any abortion should be illegal and the perpetrator subject to punishment under the laws of the land. On the other hand are those who believe, as a matter of conscience, that any abortion at any time agreed to by a woman and her doctor should be no concern of society and that society has no interest in the unborn child at any time until the moment after birth.
The people we are not hearing from are the vast majority who hold a view somewhere between those two, who believe that a woman with sound medical advice and support should be able to decide at a certain point, according to her own conscience, whether she is able, physically, mentally and emotionally, to not only give birth to but to provide for the life of a child. They also believe that there comes a time in a pregnancy where another life is involved and must be considered. I am not convinced this bill is even a good starting point from which to develop such a law.
The Canada Health Act guarantees Canadians that health services will be universal, accessible and comprehensive. If the government is bringing forward a bill, and it has, that makes abortion legal under certain conditions and under fairly broad conditions, then it must ensure that women have equal access to safe, quality medical care when they choose to exercise their rights under the law. It is not good enough to say, as the justice minister did, that it is a provincial decision as to what medical services are to be provided in their jurisdiction. When one says that Prince Edward Island, for example, has the right to fund or not fund abortion services, what one is really saying is that if somebody can afford to go

November 21, 1989
Government Orders
somewhere else is what it comes down to, then they have a right to exercise their legitimate entitlement under the law, and others who cannot afford it cannot exercise that entitlement.
This bill fails to guarantee access to a service that the bill says is perfectly legal under the right conditions. It provides the same punishment for a totally unqualified, perhaps unscrupulous practitioner who will take advantage of vulnerable women as it provides for a fully qualified medical doctor providing the same service and perhaps not quite meeting the requirements of the law. I find that inadequate protection for women from unscrupulous practitioners.

I want to address the balance of my remarks to a serious issue that is not covered in this bill and that I do not expect to be covered in any companion legislation that there is even the remotest hope of this government introducing. I want to address some of the fundamental factors that lead women to the point of feeling desperate when they find themselves pregnant and convinced that abortion is their only remedy. Abortion is the failure of social policy, of health policy and of economic policy. It is the failure of a society to adequately reflect, in its allocation of resources, in its laws and in its programs, a full and abundant respect and love for human life at all stages.

Madam Speaker, I see every day in my own riding that the society we live in does not recognize the worth and dignity of every human being.
While we are trying to decide whether we must limit or prohibit abortion, provincial governments continue to restrict access to contraception to those who can afford it. Indeed, the health insurance plans of these governments do not include contraceptives. How can we, in all good conscience, allow this abuse to continue?

How can we say on the one hand we are criminalizing abortion and yet at the same time allow people across this country not to have access to the contraceptive devices, advice and counselling that would prevent the need for an abortion?
A third point I want to make on the bill specifically is that whatever are a person's rights under the law, they have a right to know what those rights are and to exercise them. They have a right to be absolutely clear about when they are performing an act which is not legal and when they are performing one which is. I think this bill fails to a large measure to provide that clarity. The lack of clarity is evident in the fact that it is presented on some occasions as a bill that gives fairly liberal choice to women in the matter of abortion and on the other hand of clarity can only leave people unsure of their their rights, unsure of their responsibilities and unsure of whether in fact they are obeying the law.

I see every day in my own community the reasons women seek to abort rather than bear a child. I see a world of work that still punishes women for wanting or needing to be both workers and mothers, that deprives them of earning potential, promotion opportunities and even a decent pension in their old age because they choose to rear and nurture children. A society that truly valued children, that truly valued the women who bear them and the raising of those children, would put its mind to finding solutions so that women can both be mothers and fulfil every other aspect of their life.


Some families living in poverty and earning only minimum wages are forced to turn to food banks because they are unable to adequately feed and clothe their children.

I see women brutalized by an abusive partner and a society that provides to them no support and no shelter. I see women left alone with their children on the breakup of a marriage, forced to give up their homes, forced perhaps to give up a job to care for their children, to try to rebuild a secure family environment for them to grow up in. I see a society that does not value their roles as mothers but through its welfare system provides poverty level support and hems them in with rules and regula-
November 21, 1989

tions that keep them and their children trapped in poverty. I see them deprived of the encouragement and support they need to become self-sufficient, left on long lists, waiting for child care and waiting for training programs.
Just this past week I received a letter that clearly outlines this from a young woman who is finally breaking out of that trap. She is back in school and has parent who is attending school, who has a goal to obtain an education in order to get a worthwhile job. If there are not sufficient subsidized day care spaces, what happens to the others like me who have this same goal?" Yet the budget clearly says that because of the fiscal situation, the government has decided not to proceed with the expenditure of $4 billion over the next seven years to increase significantly the number of good and quality child care spaces across Canada.
That is a plea from a woman, who is making her way in the world, that we provide what is necessary for others like her to do the same.

Women are trapped in a social system which deprives them of life's essentials and does not help them become self-sufficient.

The statistics speak for themselves. Families headed by women are four times as likely to be poor than families headed by men. At the same time as these women struggle I see them and their families, their children, shunned and condemned by a society that brands them and their children as leeches on the generosity of society, responsible for all the ills of their communities, responsible through the social programs even for the national debt.
I see women out in the workforce struggling to support themselves and their children but unable to earn a decent living because they are trapped in pink collar ghettos where pay Women still earn only 66 cents for every dollar a man earns.
Most heartbreakingly I see the children of poverty entering our school system with three strikes against them, judged as incapable before they are even five years old because they are not as well nourished, not as well dressed, their hair is not as bright and shiny and they do not speak the same way as children from better off famlies do. Is it any wonder, branded as failures, they drop out of school at a rate double that of the general
Government Orders
population? It is vicious cycle as poor incomes lead to dropping out of school which results in poor incomes which leads to the next generation dropping out of school.
In this, one of the wealthiest countries in the world, we have over one million children, one of every six children, living in a family where the income is below the poverty level. And two-thirds of children raised by female single parents are poor.
I see a justice system that punishes theft more severely than it punishes the sexual abuse of a child. I see our children bombarded by a society that uses the sexuality of women to sell products in the marketplace. Yet I see people who do not want to see sexuality and birth control even discussed in our schools. I see young girls who become sexually active while they are still children, seeking some small token of self-worth in a society that tells them that being sexy and glamorous is the way to have value and importance and in many areas they still are told that only men achieve success and value.
I see neighbourhoods where showers are held for 13-year old pregnant girls because when the predominant climate of the community is poverty and hopelessness, the birth of a child is a reason to have some new hope.
The public debate on abortion has been so polarized around the question of birth that it has to a large extent obliterated the question of life. I would love at some point in my stay in this Parliament to have as many phone calls and as many letters addressing the issues of poverty for women and children as I have had on this issue.
The polarization on one end has been focused on giving women the legal and theoretical right to choose not to bear a child. I have chosen to address those factors that rob women of choices, that make it impossible for them to choose pregnancy with joy and with hope.
On the other end the debate has focused on the right of a child to be bom but not on the right of every child to be nurtured, supported and valued to fully develop its humanity at every stage of life.
There are many things that have been said and will be said about this bill, and I do not need to repeat them all. Whether by placing the onus on doctors for meeting some nebulous criteria we ensure that more and more doctors in fact choose not to risk their careers and their practice by making a decision that is somewhat ill-defined; whether doctors are subject to private actions that call into question their judgment as medical practitioners; whether pregnant women can still be dragged publicly through the courts, every detail of their private

November 21, 1989
Government Orders
lives flashed on the television, radio and the newspapers; whether the bill fails to adequately respect the developing human life; whether it forces women to lie and deceive to achieve a right which the law at least on the surface gives them; whether it gives a choice to women of economic means and not to women who do not have the same economic advantages; whether the issue could not be dealt with more thoroughly in the Health Act where it could be combined with measures on contraception, on counselling, on options and on various other related matters; whether this bill describes with sufficient clarity the rights and responsibilities of women and their doctors; whether in fact the bill is any more than a duplicitous attempt to please both sides, without really addressing the issues, society at large feels the need to be addressed.
It is difficult but necessary, I think, not to be guided by our private moral values, by the conscience that we would apply in our own lives to choices that we might personally have to make but to act as legislators with respect for the belief of others who perhaps have different standards and different moral values. We must act with compassion for those who find themselves in a situation in which certainly most of us in this House would never find ourselves, and with a commitment to do that which respects the pluralism of our society and the democratic principle that the laws will not force the moral beliefs of one segment of society on all of society except where society itself is directly threatened. It is clear that we do not know what the predominant moral value in society is on this.
I started out by saying it is a difficult question. It is a difficult question. I urge us all to act with that respect, that compassion and that commitment to a law which respects the diversity of views that Canadians have on this subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened carefully to the member and I am still not sure what her position is on this bill. I guess that probably goes for her party as well. I wanted to ask this question of the minister who has left the House. The minister said a little earlier that each Canadian woman will be entitled to a medical abortion and will be able to have it with dignity as a result
of this legislation. I wonder if she agrees with that, if that is her interpretation of the limits? Well, really this bill has no limits as far as access is concerned which is what the minister, I think, was saying.
The member mentioned some examples in the form of questions. I wondered about the example of women, for various reasons, seeking abortions which doctors do not judge to be for health reasons. She was indicating that doctors may be feeling that they have to have a very strict interpretation of "health" under this act. The member mentioned young people whose health is not in danger but who simply cannot care for a child and who have many reasons for not wanting to continue with the pregnancy. She mentioned single women who are healthy but become pregnant and do not want to bear a child for various reasons. She mentioned as well low-income women who may have several children and simply cannot cope financially with an abortion. All these examples would probably be women who are not seeking abortions strictly for health reasons and therefore, I assume, would be not eligible for a legal abortion under this bill and doctors indeed might be fearful of giving too liberal an interpretation of the question of health. I would like the member's views on this.

Madam Speaker, the member has raised a myriad of questions which may require another 20-minute speech in which to reply. It is true that the Liberal party does not have a position on abortion. It has done what I think is the right thing and allowed each member to vote according to his or her own conscience. I think that is an appropriate approach on a bill such as this.
If the member detected no firm commitment one way or another on this bill, she is absolutely right. I have a number of reservations with the bill. I have not yet concluded whether, in fact, it is worth allowing a bill like this to proceed through second reading to committee stage where it might be improved and some of the issues she raised addressed. That is why I am paying very close attention to all the debates in the House and to a number of other people whose advice I am seeking.

Obviously I do not believe that this bill gives women equal access everywhere in the country, regardless of their financial circumstances, to what the bill purports to deliver as a legal right and entitlement for them. I do not want to comment on how the law will be interpreted. I suspect that the Minister of Justice knows quite well that under this law there is virtually no possibility of a doctor or a woman being prosecuted and convicted for the carrying out of an abortion.

Madam Speaker, I have a number of questions I would like to ask the member. I am particularly struck by her last comment because I think people are playing ostrich. They are putting their heads in the sand and passing criminal legislation and then saying, "Let's not worry about it because a doctor is never going to be prosecuted under this act".
The reality is that doctors are going to be prosecuted. People who are anti-choice are going to be trying desperately to have a doctor charged and doctors are going to become fearful. This bill does not allow an abortion for a 14-year-old-girl. It does not allow abortions for deformity of a foetus. It does not allow abortions for incest. It does not allow abortions for family planning or socioeconomic reasons. People said that if a young girl went to a doctor and the doctor said that he would not perform an abortion, she need only go to another doctor. The first doctor has made a decision that the abortion could be subject to criminal sanction because there is not a threat to the woman's health. Now is the second doctor going to perform that abortion? I doubt it. If no doctor is ever going to be charged, why do you think they are putting it in the Criminal Code? Is it not the intent to put it in the Criminal Code so that if people step over the bounds they will be charged?

Mr. Speaker, I think the member misunderstands. I am not the person proposing this legislation and I think those comments and questions should more appropriately be addressed to the minister who did propose it and I trust that he either has done or will be doing that.

Madam Speaker, when the Supreme Court struck down the existing criminal legislation on abortion almost two years ago Justice Wilson said at the time, and I quote: "The right to reproduce or not to produce-is properly perceived as
Government Orders
an integral part of modem woman's straggle to assert her dignity and worth as a human being."
I completely agree with this and I and my Party take this principle as the starting point in any serious discussion about the right to abortion.
The problem today in our country is not that we no longer have criminal legislation respecting abortion, the real problem today is that Canadian women do not have assured access to abortion services. They are denied the dignity that Justice Wilson specifically wrote about.
The bill we have before us does nothing to change that. What it does is confront women with the threat of criminal prosecution. What it does is reduce women's right and ability to make decisions that affect their lives. The New Democratic Party of Canada cannot accept such legislation.
Women have varying philosophical and religious beliefs about abortion. That is obvious. Some are totally opposed for reasons that I respect, if I do not agree with them. Others believe it ought to be their right to decide. We believe as a matter of policy, I believe as a matter of principle, it is not for the state to legislate one answer for everyone. The state must provide a legal framework for all women to choose freely according to their own philosophy or their own religious convictions. This bill does not do this.
Quite the contrary. It makes abortion illegal except for women who fit certain health criteria. It reduces access to abortion by threatening doctors with criminal action. It makes women possible accessories to a crime. It invites third party interventions. It in no way addresses prevention or unwanted pregnancies. For those who believe morality is based on freedom, as do I, this bill must be defeated.

Let us be frank! Women faced with an unwanted pregnancy under this legislation might feel compelled to claim they are weak or under trauma in order to qualify for abortion. They would need their physician's judgment. If the physician refused, they would have to seek another one. And where a first physician had refused to induce the abortion, would a second one take the opposing view thereby taking the risk of being charged under the criminal code? Certainly or probably not. The legislation is unfair to medical practitioners. It forces

November 21, 1989
Government Orders
them to make decisions they would rather not make. But, it is deeply unfair to women.
The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court at the time of the same ruling that I quoted earlier had this to say:
Forcing a woman, by threat of criminal sanction, to carry a foetus to term unless she meets certain criteria unrelated to her own priorities and aspirations, is a profound interference with a woman's body and thus a violation of security of the person.
Women must have the right to be free in reaching a decision themselves in this domain, obviously, after consultation with loved ones in a particular case, after consultation for medical purposes with their doctors, after consultation with any range of a number of people that they may want to discuss the situation with, if they so desire in terms of moral considerations involved. But the fundamental human right-and I stress human right-ought to reside with a woman to decide. The bill denies Canadian women that right. Therefore it is unacceptable for this reason.
The bill should also be rejected because it does not guarantee access. Those women who have been denied abortions because of the control of hospital therapeutic abortion boards by those opposed to choice may be no better off as a result of this legislation. They can still be denied access to what I regard as a fundamental human right, as does the Supreme Court.
Poor women will suffer. Wealthy and powerful women have always had access to abortion, and always will. Throughout the whole history of civilized existence, when abortion was at one time condoned by the church, after it had ceased to be condoned by the church, when abortion was deemed to be unacceptable for a variety of secular reasons in certain societies, those with wealth and power, women with wealth, have always had access to an effective right to an abortion if they wanted it. The reality is that money has bought freedom. Money has bought choice. I believe that freedom, whether in this domain or any other, should not be dependent on wealth. That ought to be a fundamental concern.

The truth is, there is no need for criminal law to regulate the morality of Canadian women on that issue.
Our mothers, sisters, wives and daughters are not criminals. In Canada, there is no need to introduce abortion into the Criminal Code. Since January 1988, abortion no longer comes under the Criminal Code. The number of abortions has not changed. But in Prince Edward Island, women still do not have access to abortion services. In Newfoundland, only one medical practitioner induces abortions in a hospital. Women in northern British Columbia, northern Alberta and northern Ontario must travel great distances to obtain an abortion. In Nova Scotia, where the number of late abortions is higher than the average, with a higher risk of health hazards, the provincial Government recently took measures to restrict still further access to abortion services.
Canadian women have no need for threats of criminal penalties. What they need is that the Canadian Government ensures they have access to abortion services.

The Canada Health Act stipulates that universality, comprehensiveness and accessibility must apply for all medically required services. Through the financial clout of the federal government, it should insist that these principles apply to the issue of abortion. The federal government, as we have made clear for a number of years now, has the legislative mandate to achieve these principles in application to the question of abortion. It is time this government showed leadership by using the Canada Health Act the way it could be used effectively to guarantee access to this important right from one coast to the other.
Despite the best intentions, some 64 per cent of pregnancies occur while partners are using some form of birth control. All methods of birth control have flaws, and any choice involves some kind of compromise, a compromise to a woman's health. Danger by and large tends to increase with the reliability of the birth control device that is used. Women who use IUDs risk pelvic inflammatory disease and sterility. Those on the pill can face two to four times the risk of heart attack and stroke.
November 21, 1989

When birth control fails-to state the obvious under such circumstances-women are faced with unwanted pregnancies. If the foetus is carried to term, women in today's society overwhelmingly continue to be the primary care givers in the family structure, and frequently for single women, the only source of financial and emotional support for the child. That is what is involved if a woman is forced to have an unwanted child.
I ask members of the House to keep in mind, if we are thinking of single women here, that 56 per cent of single-parent families in this country live at or below the poverty level. Knowing this reality, I repeat, a woman ought to have the right to freely decide for herself in such a situation.
Family planning organizations all over the country have long recognized women's lack of control over their own fertility as a major health risk for themselves and for their families.
Pregnancy in women 15 to 19 years of age is considered to be the number one health problem by many health specialists. Teenage mothers experience a higher rate of mortality and morbidity. Pregnancy in adolescent women can seriously interrupt educational goals and often results, as we all know too well, in lifelong poverty. Young women who become pregnant after discussing all options, again I repeat, must be free to choose.
We have come a long way since 1969 when we threw out laws that made it illegal to disseminate information on birth control. But this bill shows we have not come far enough.
One woman in four is sexually active in our society on this continent and in northern Europe by 15 years of age. It is time we all understood that. Fewer than 10 per cent of North American teenagers use an effective method of birth control when they first become sexually active. In contrast, 90 per cent of adolescents in Scandinavian countries use birth control methods from the start.
Quebec, a province with one of the best birth control services in North America, also happens to have one of the lowest rates of unwanted pregnancy in the country. A child bom in the province of Quebec tends to be a wanted child. We believe all children bom in Canada ought to be wanted children.

Hear, hear!
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, the Family Planning Division of Health and Welfare Canada is composed of one full-time staff person. Surely this must change. Surely the federal government must make a substantial increase in the funding of birth control education and all other aspects of family planning in this country.
I want to conclude this brief but serious speech on this very serious subject by saying that families, as all of us know, can be the source of infinite joy, of boundless love, of security and of kinship. The decision to bring children into this world is quite possibly the most serious decision a man and a woman together-a woman in the ultimate sense here-will ever make. Such a decision, with all its responsibility implied, should be a free decision.
Let us not enact a bill that would make criminals of women who do not look lightly upon the responsibilities in such a choice. Let us do all we can instead to ensure that all children in Canada are wanted children.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, I listened with care to the very serious speech that the member for Oshawa just made. I would ask him if he is telling the House by implication, taking his premise that abortion should be exclusively a matter between a woman and her doctor, that society or the government, if you like, has at no point the right to interfere with that, to regulate that matter. Or, in other words, is he telling the House that at 16, 20, or 22 weeks it is still his view and that of his party that society has not the right to say, at some stage: "You cannot make the decision exclusively between the two of you"?

I am saying that of course we need regulations in this domain, but they are health regulations. The evidence is overwhelming that we do not need criminal law.
We have criminal law in our society and in others, if there is a mode of behaviour, a kind of behaviour that is deemed to be repulsive or morally unacceptable, and we need the sanction of criminal law to curtail. The evidence is overwhelming in this particular area that we are now debating that criminal law is not required, that Canadian women, as I said in my comments, whether they are our friends, wives, sisters, mothers, or lovers, are responsible, moral human beings. They have so

Government Orders
demonstrated it in the case of the country as a whole since the Supreme Court decision almost two years ago.
Also, in the case of the Province of Quebec, where there has been freedom of choice for many years before that, there has not been irresponsibility-if one chooses a word-to deal with the issue in moral choices made by women.
Overwhelmingly, the decisions made about pregnancies are in the earliest stages. Overwhelmingly, when they occur late in a pregnancy, it is to save the woman's life, or for some other very serious medical reason involving deformities that may occur.
The evidence for us, not only in this party, but for the large majority of Canadian women, I repeat, is that we do not need Criminal Code sanctions, with all the attendant risks that come with such a measure in this domain.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the hon. member for Oshawa. It is a follow-up to the question my friend from Edmonton just asked. I know this is a very serious issue and he and I, as he obviously knows, will disagree strongly, our positions being naturally very different.
I want to get it clear in my mind if the member is telling us that at no point in the pregnancy does he think that society has an interest of such a magnitude that criminal law should apply, that at no point in the pregnancy is there an offence against society if the life of the unborn were terminated. In fact, that is criminal law-it is an offence against society. My colleague is a lawyer, and I am sure he knows that far better than I.
He is not a lawyer. He is a professor.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party

I am sorry, he is not a lawyer. Neither am

I want to ask him very seriously if the position that he is taking is that at no point in the pregnancy is that the case. Madam Speaker, let me begin my clearing the record. I have many faults, but being a member of the legal profession is not among them.
On the substantive matter, as I said earlier, my understanding of the principle of why criminal law is needed is that certain modes of behaviour become not only repulsive but the instrument of the state is needed to ensure that they do not take place. The evidence as we have seen it in our own country is that the kind of outrageous act envisioned by the hon. member-and perhaps he might think of a woman having an abortion at the latest steps, beyond a certain point in the development of the foetus-does not take place. Therefore, if there is no evidence that this practice is taking place, from our point of view you do not need the sanction of a moral code. You do not need to leave the implication, as it would for me, that women are not exercising their moral responsibility seriously when I believe they are.
If there were a situation that is hypothetically possible along the lines that the hon. member alludes to, and he has acknowledged a philosophical conception, a view that fundamentally differs from mine-and I repeat that I respect that difference quite seriously even though I do not share it-if we are evolved in our behaviour as a society, and if we consider the kinds of practices that he alludes to as being hypothetically possible, then perhaps hypothetically at some point you might need that.
Why make that assumption now when there is no evidence to warrant it? The evidence goes very clearly all in the opposite direction that women, like men, are morally responsible human beings and therefore ought to have the right, in my view, to continue to exercise their freedom unfettered by the potential threat of the Criminal Code.
all members of the House that if you want to protect the unborn, you protect their mothers. That is how you do it.
Hear, hear!

I have a question for the hon. member for Oshawa because I want him to expand on one particular area of his remarks. He said that the woman should have the right to freely decide this matter of having an abortion.
I would like to ask him this question because there are some people who already feel that under this proposed legislation women would have that unfettered right, they would be able to freely decide in consultation with their doctors whether they are going to have an abortion. They say that because, as some people say, the criteria are so wide that you could drive a Sherman tank through them. I ask the hon. member for Oshawa why he would be concerned about women not having this unfettered right to make this decision once this legislation were passed, if it were to be passed.

I would be veiy happy to answer that question. As the member knows, the criteria is essentially medical. It seems to me that it is something that ought to concern us from a point of view of moral responsibility. We are doing precisely what I believe the Supreme Court and this legislation has ultimately tested. There is better than a fifty-fifty chance that it will be declared ultra vires because it does deny the basic rights of a woman in terms of free choice, independent of medical criteria, to make a decision.
I will just repeat in my answer the argumentation that I found both moving and logically cogent in the ruling of the Chief Justice. He said: "Forcing a woman by threat of criminal sanction to carry a foetus to term unless she meets certain criteria unrelated to her own priorities and aspirations-" There is no reference to health, physical or psychological. He says: "-unrelated to her own priorities and aspirations is a profound interference with a woman's body and thus a violation of security of the person".
That is a very cogent expression of the view that a woman ought to have the unfettered right to decide. If I were involved, if my wife were pregnant, we would have this discussion. I believe this myself.
