Our party's position is a question of a choice here. I am saying as an extension of that principle, if I advised my wife that I did not favour her having an abortion, even as a partner in the act of creating a potential human being, then she should be free ultimately to reject it. I believe that. She ought to have that right. Certainly, she should not, nor should any other person, married or unmarried, have to go to a doctor for other than medical reasons. If a doctor says there are good medical reasons for a woman not to have an abortion, then that opinion should be respected.
The woman should not have to be dependent upon anyone's opinion, medically, psychologically or whatever, if she is to have the respect, as the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada said, to her security as a person, her ultimate freedom. We have to give her that freedom. We ought not to deal with the question again, having legislation that refers to medical criteria basically as the only criteria to be used in reaching such a decision.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I rise to take part in this debate it goes without saying that members of all sides of the House face a dilemma. Can we support with our vote a bill that we may find difficult to support in our hearts and in our minds?
At the outset, it is important that the country observing this debate recognize and accept that as legislators we have the duty not only to vote but to speak, to explain our votes. The two go together. So, in my comments today, I ask members and my constituents not only to note that I support this bill, but also to remember why I do.
We must remember where we were in this House on this issue in the summer of 1988. The House faced an obligation imposed on it by the Supreme Court following its decision in Morgentaler to come to a consensus on a new law on abortion, a law that would balance the rights of women desiring an abortion and the rights of the unborn child.
The House faced an opportunity, an opportunity to choose from a variety of approaches to a new law. We failed to achieve a consensus. That process proved what we knew then and we know now. There is no agreement in this country. There is no agreement in this House.

Government Orders
Possibly there is no agreement in any party on what an ideal abortion regime in Canada should be.
Agonizing as it has been, futile as it appeared, the process in my mind was useful. It was useful if only to demonstrate through our imperfect means in this place that no one's ideal law can be achieved in this place.
The government has done what it had to do in the context I have just described. It has introduced for debate, for study, for possible amendment and finally a vote, a bill that attempts to balance the rights to security of the person of the woman seeking an abortion and the right to life of the unborn.
Simply, as I see it, the bill does this by beginning with the premise that an abortion cannot be performed unless it is necessary to preserve the health of the woman. It removes the previous procedural obstacles that the Supreme Court indicated infringed on the security of the person of the woman and which has been part of this debate in earlier speeches.
The bill, in acknowledging that abortion is a medical procedure, places on the medical practitioner the responsibility of determining whether the procedure is medically warranted. I do not shy away from placing that responsibility on those who are trained, those who are professional and those who must make life and death decisions in the course of their work every day.
But in my view the bill does not adequately circumscribe the grounds on which the act of terminating unborn life should be allowed. From my perspective and that of many Canadians of every region, both men and women-and I believe from every walk of life-this is the bill's greatest deficiency. It will be said that the bill allows abortions for too wide a variety of motives and under too many circumstances. I freely admit that such a prospect troubles me deeply.
In response, however, I can only point out the inherent weakness of the law, of any law, not just this law. How does law deal with the motives of the human being? For the law to command respect and to have any effect it must do two things.
First, it must bear some relation to things as they are, and not exclusively as they should be. Second, it must be capable of enforcement.
I have come to the conclusion, though reluctantly, that no abortion law would be capable of preventing abortion on the scale on which it occurs in our society today, and that no law would reverse what has been done in our society for the previous 20 years.
I believe that women seeking an abortion are not going to change their intentions if a law imposes a threat to their health or their freedom. Is a remedy a sanction against the woman? Remember, we are dealing, my colleagues, with criminal law. A sanction can only take place after an act has been committed. For those of us who are pro life it does not address the saving of life.
Physicians are not going to deny abortions to women whose health is affected by the pregnancy as they determine it in their professional code. Regrettably, juries are not going to convict today any more than they have in the past.
I acknowledge that our society does not respect unborn life sufficiently. I acknowledge further that in general our society inadequately supports women who bear children. As a former Minister of National Health and Welfare I struggled with the issue of what type of programs could we come forward with which would strengthen the support for women and with it the support for the family. I agree that in general men have a long way to go in respecting and placing sufficient value on the roles of parenting and caring for children.
This debate is not simply a woman's debate or an issue relating to or affecting women only. It affects women, obviously. It affects men. It affects children. These failings of our society are not going to be solved in this law or any other because the law cannot reform the human heart, and too often we try here to do just that. The law cannot achieve what society is unwilling or incapable of achieving.
We freely admit that the state cannot solve the great issues of human life. Many of us know that genuine reform in society will not come through political reform. Yet I believe that the state has a moral obligation to restrain the actions taken by men.
Chuck Colson in his book Kingdoms and Conflict writes the following: "Attitudes are forged by spiritual forces, not by legislation. Values change when spiritual move-
November 21, 1989

ments stir the hearts of people and when fresh winds of reason stir their minds."
I am also convinced that we need a law because virtually every action, individual or corporate, in society is circumscribed in some manner by law, no matter how minimal the protection or the sanctions within that law. Surely members on both sides of this issue would have to agree that this issue is of sufficient import that if other actions are circumscribed by law, this action of abortion is sufficiently serious to be considered to be circumscribed by law as well.
What I do believe, therefore, is that what this proposed law will do is reinforce the principle that human life has unique value; that unborn life cannot be terminated simply on the basis of one person's choice without recognized grounds. Therefore I support this bill, albeit after much struggle and soul searching for two more fundamental reasons.
The first alternative was to have a law that rests on the principle that unborn life somehow attains greater value with the passage of time. The cabinet, and I say this even though we are all restricted by cabinet confidences, struggled with that issue. This House struggles with that issue. I am absolutely convinced that if we ever accept the principle that life somehow gains value as it matures, we are then subject to that great danger of asking ourselves the question: Does life lose value as it ages?
The second reason for supporting this law is that the alternative is no law. That, to me, is unacceptable because underlying such a course of action is the principle that unborn life has no value at all. It needs to be said in this place that the kind of solution for a middle ground proposed by the Law Refrom Commission, namely a gestational principle, is arbitrary in moral and scientific terms. Arbitrariness is precisely what the law is supposed to prevent. That was one option open to the government. I am pleased and frankly relieved that that course of action has not been taken.
This bill maintains that there are no stages in the value of life. If there were, then any other stage of life would be subject to arbitrary evaluation. If we introduce the idea of relativism in this matter, it will be difficult to exclude it in other matters. The whole concept of human rights rests on the principle of excluding arbitrariness and relativism.
Government Orders
A bill based on the gestational principle could have been one alternative, but the House would have faced the same dilemma it faces now, a membership comprised of those who believe that the law is not even necessary, of those who believe a law must prevent abortions under any circumstances except for a threat to the mother's life, and of those who favour a law that allows abortions in some cases. No bill, I am convinced, would be capable of covering that spectrum. The point, therefore, is that we have this bill and we have to decide what to do with it.
The alternative to this bill, the result of a negative vote, would be a complete absence of any signal by society or to society that abortion is a serious matter involving human life.
The proposal has been called a compromise bill and I suppose it is. I think of it rather as an incomplete bill. It is incomplete because it rests on what is outside the law for its force and its effectiveness, namely, the values that thousands of Canadians bring each year to the decision of abortion. It is incomplete because it does not contain all the protection for human life, for unborn life, that I would like personally to see contained in abortion law. It is incomplete because perhaps society will ever yet move to a greater respect for human life in every dimension.
Possibly in the not distant future, in a more perfect and caring world, public attitudes and the public institutions by which we govern ourselves will respect the most innocent and vulnerable of human life. It will be a society which celebrates the fact that we have been given the joy not only the obligation of experiencing divine creation and giving support to that divine life in all its stages. Regrettably that day is not today.
Therefore I have not been persuaded by the arguments of my colleagues on the other side of this issue and I, in turn, have failed to persuade them with my arguments. However here we are with the best that the government could do, the best that the House could do, and I think the best that society could do on this issue in law at this time.
All of us have been influenced by certain forces. We all are influenced by what we have experienced and what we have been taught. On this issue I have been influenced by the British parliamentarian Wilberforce

November 21, 1989
Government Orders
who, as my colleagues will know, was instrumental in having the slave trade abolished in the United Kingdom in the early 1800s. Wilberforce struggled with the need to compromise in public life as well as the obligation to be faithful to his faith. In that struggle his clergyman, a minister by the name of Newton, a member of the Church of England, gave Wilberforce some advice. Wilberforce was saying: "I have to compromise too much in public life and I might as well leave public life and do something else."
Wilberforce, after he had spoken to Newton, took the counsel of Newton, who said very simply: "You follow your own faith, your own convictions, but you do not abandon public office." Wilberforce followed that advice, Madam Speaker, and I intend to do the same.
And so it takes me to my last point. What can we do tonight? I am convinced that the law will not change the hearts of men and women. I am convinced as well that the law will not change the fact that 65,000 young Canadians die each year. I have to recognize that. I also have to recognize that sanctions are not the answer.
Therefore, I challenge the churches, I challenge the men and women in society to put faith to action: Adopt an unborn child. Let us take away the stigma that just because a child is unwanted that that child should therefore have no future. I have seen churches adopt children. I have seen them take under their care unwed mothers, give them care, give them support, give them a future. I have come to the conclusion that it is men and women in that setting who will have to become the answer to helping those who are most vulnerable and, in so doing, be that leaven, that catalyst in society that society can pride itself in preserving life.
It is with those conditions that I support this bill.

I have a comment and a question for the hon. member for Provencher who I know has struggled authentically with the various responsibilities that come in public life-tension between one's own individual conscience, the view of one's particular religious community, the view of one's political party, the view of one's constituents, and all those things that go together to make being in this place sometimes a very difficult place to be, particularly when it comes to an issue like this one.
Without entering into debate about the member's reasons for indicating his support for this bill, I was only moved to rise at the end when, if I remember him correctly, he threw out a challenge to the church and presumably to all those in the Christian community who out of their Christian belief have taken a pro-life position and who have advocated either a position similar to the one that this legislation which we have before us represents, or a position which is even more restrictive with respect to abortion, and I expect something like the member for Provencher might have advocated in another context.
When I heard the word "challenge", what I was hoping for-and I do not say this in any polemical way-was not that the challenge would only be to individual families or churches to adopt, but that the challenge would be to society to create the social and economic conditions in which women could choose life, choose pregnancy, without as it is the case in so many cases choosing poverty. If we want to send signals about the value that we place on children, we do that every time we make law with respect to family allowances, we do that every time we make law or we don't with respect to child care, and we do that every time we make law with respect to unemployment insurance and make a distinction between the benefits that adoptive parents get and natural parents.
There are a host of ways in which the concern that the member for Provencher raised could be more comprehensively articulated. I think that is the challenge which ought to be issued to those churches that find themselves at odds with this law or that advocate a stricter law.
In that respect I have to say to the member that many times when certain churches have been involved in advocating certain social and economic policies they have been told by successive governments that it is not any of their business, that these are matters for economists.
I hope we could at least agree that it is not just a question of individual action with respect to adoption. It is also a question of social and economic policies, both sending signals to potential parents as to how supportive society is going to be of their choice to be parents in whatever context that choice is exercised and to society in general. It seems to me that that is where the challenge should go out to the churches and to the Christian community or, for that matter, to any other religious community. They ought to teach not by the

force of law in this case but by the power of example, by the power of love exercised not just individually but through the civil community, and by the other laws that might be passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, to answer that question would take a lot of time, and in the issues of human life there is never one answer.
I know the member asked the question in the spirit that I have seen him address this question at other times. There is no doubt in my mind that social or economic circumstances have an effect on the decisions we take, but I would caution him, if I might, in the same spirit that it is not necessarily those in the lower economic groups who seek abortions today in Canada. I think we should be careful with that.
Perhaps I could use a personal example. I do it with a great amount of hesitation, but I do it perhaps to make the point. As I said earlier we come from our own experiences. I am a member of a family of four and I am the only one who is not adopted. My father and his first wife adopted two children who are brother and sister naturally and who escaped the Soviet Union. One was four and the other five. That family was very poor. The children were advertised in a church newspaper. It had very little to do with economics. It had everything to do with attitude.
My mother and her first husband adopted a girl. My mother's first husband for their entire married life was ill. They adopted a girl. All I am saying is that we should be careful when we give to this question that easy economic answer.
When I take a look at our native people, if I may speak about them for a moment, their attitudes to life and the reality of their poverty, I find very different attitudes in that society than I find in the general mainstream of Canadian society.
I do not want to deflect from the member's comments and his question, so I come back to the question. I say to him that I believe that not only the Christian churches but society in general should not ascribe to society the powers that it does not have. I believe that society only sets frameworks through law. People then work within that framework to do good or to do evil. I have tried to challenge them to do one of the greatest goods, and that is take from their own resources both financial, physical, emotional, spiritual and help someone rather than simply condemn because either the law is not good enough
Government Orders
or that society does not understand or want to understand.
I appreciate what the gentleman says when he talks about economic factors. I am sure they play into that from time to time with certain circumstances, but I would suggest they do not affect every case or every decision relating to abortion.

I did not mean to suggest-and I think the record will show it-that every case is affected only by economic factors. I tried to go beyond that. For instance, with respect to child care, in many cases the need or the prospective lack of child care is something which affects decisions about parenthood, decisions made not only by the poor but by middle income and upper income Canadian women who have to make decisions about whether or not they would have to leave their job in order to provide the kind of care that they may think is unavailable because of the current child care system or may be unavailable to them depending on where they live or for a variety of circumstances.
I certainly was not meaning to suggest that it is only poor women who seek abortions, although in many cases economics are a very strong element in why people make the decisions that they make, and we know that to be a fact.
All I am saying is that when it is a question of pure economics and choosing poverty by choosing pregnancy, or when it is a question of other things that may come into the factors in the decision-making process by women who we would not consider poor, all these things are related to social policy decisions that we make on other days in this House of Commons.
The challenge that the member issued at the end of his speech to the church should be a challenge not only to do the individual moral thing of being available to adopt children who may be unwanted, but the social, moral thing of being involved in the political process in building up the kind of support networks that would enable all women, regardless of their circumstances, to make the kind of choices that the hon. member wants them to make.

That is why I come back to the main thesis of my point tonight, and that is, yes, let us strive to get a society that is more equitable, but let us never ascribe to society the ability to change the moral factors which I believe are personal

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with some pleasure and very serious intent that I rise this evening to join in this debate on Bill C-43.
Perhaps I might just comment on the speech of my colleague, the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, because nothing shows more clearly the difficulties faced by members in this House. The hon. member is a colleague whom I love and admire very much and whom I am proud to stand beside and on most days sit behind as a colleague of this House. Yet, he and I take very different views on the issue which is the subject of the bill being debated this evening.
I think we can understand that when trusted and loyal colleagues take very different views on an issue such as this one-and it is truly a divisive issue indeed-not only does it not lend itself to the kinds of usual partisan organization that we find in this House, but it is a profound challenge to our understanding of our role as parliamentarians to find some common ground to meet the expectations of Canadians that we will make some kind of sense out of one of the most divisive issues in society today.
Like my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, my position on the issue of abortion itself is well known in my community where I am well known as an advocate of those who are pro-choice. Like the hon. minister, I face the challenge of going into my community and trying to reconcile views that are basically irreconcilable on this fundamental issue.
My particular perspective on this issue of abortion arises from my own experience and my own intellectual and spiritual development. As a philosophical Conservative, I have a great distaste for dealing with human problems in the abstract. I am often reminded of the statement of Edmund Burke, perhaps one of the great founders of philosophical conservatism, in his commentary on the French Revolution written in 1790 that the French revolutionaries saw men as abstractions and in seeing them as abstractions they forget that they were
human. It has been one of the guiding principles of my life to try never to lose sight of the human dimension of an issue.
In the issue of abortion there are a number of human dimensions but, in particular, it is an issue that lends itself very poorly to attempts to generalize or to understand in the abstract. I am reminded also of the opening lines of Tolstoy's great novel Anna Karenina, where he says words to the effect that all happy families are alike; unhappy families are each unhappy in their own way. I think similarly one could say that all welcome pregnancies are in a sense alike; but each unwanted pregnancy is unwanted in its own way. The existence of an unwanted pregnancy is a circumstance that is unique to the woman involved.
I am among those Canadians who are very comfortable without a law because from my perspective I feared a law which would attempt to generalize about what is basically an experience that cannot be generalized. I feared that we would not be able to come up with a law that would respect the uniqueness of the decision to terminate or continue a pregnancy.
Bill C-43 has been described as a compromise law. Certainly for those who are on the pro-choice side of the issue the fundamental compromise is whether to have a law or not. As I say, I dreaded the prospect of a law in this area because I feared very deeply the notion of trying to create a legal framework that would lose sight of the unique circumstances that are involved in each decision with respect to pregnancy. But I can say quite sincerely and with quite a clear heart that I believe that this bill is actually better than no law. I realize that this is a position which will come as a surprise to many people who share my position on the fundamental issue of abortion. I want to address myself this evening to the reasons why I, as a very committed and passionate pro-choicer, can support Bill C-43.
I believe that in order to have a law there has to be some quid pro quo and the law itself has to respect the privacy, and, as I say, the uniqueness of the decision that has to be made about a pregnancy. I believe this bill does

both. It certainly describes abortion as fundamentally a decision made by a woman with her doctor.
Unlike many people on the pro-choice side of the issue, I am not at all uncomfortable with the role of the doctor in that decision because I believe that what the bill describes as the legal framework within which abortion is performed is fundamentally good medical practice. The definition of "health" is very broad and I believe takes into account all of the circumstances in which a woman would seek an abortion.
But I would be very disturbed by a regime which did not require of medical practitioners that an opinion be formed before the procedure be carried out because just as I am deeply opposed to the notion of a woman not being able to obtain an abortion when she wants it, I think it is equally tragic for a woman to have an abortion which she later regrets. Now, that is part of human life and we all do things which we may later regret, but I think it is extremely important that when a woman goes to a doctor with a request for something as serious as a termination of a pregnancy that there at least be an inquiry as to whether that decision is an informed decision, whether it is based on a realistic evaluation of her circumstance.
I give as an example an older woman who is pregnant who may go to a doctor and may otherwise not be averse to having a child but may be convinced that at her age she will undoubtedly produce a deformed child. Some reassurance from a doctor about the diagnostic techniques of amniocentesis, for example, may be very helpful there. A woman who is in an emotional state because she fears she will be left by her partner because she is pregnant may want to reconsider that decision in light of broader options that are available to her.
So I think what is described in the bill, the requirement that a doctor form an opinion based on standard medical practice is simply good medical practice and it is something that all women are entitled to. I do not find that a problem at all.
What I think is extremely useful about the bill and what for me tips the balance in terms of this bill as opposed to no law is that I believe that in so far as it is possible for the federal government to take steps to ensure access to abortion, this bill does so by clarifying
Government Orders
abortion as a medical procedure performed for health reasons.
It has been stated by many people in the House during this debate, including my colleagues the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Justice, that the federal government has no jurisdiction to regulate health practice in Canada.
Contrary to the understanding of many Canadians, the Canada Health Act is not a statute regulating health, it is a funding statute by which the federal government basically intrudes into the area of provincial jurisdiction with its spending power. So the notion that somehow one could put a provision into the Canada Health Act that would assure access to abortion is a mistaken notion, relying on a failure to understand the realities of Canadian constitutional law.
I believe that this law accomplishes perhaps the one good thing that was accomplished by the law that was struck down in the Morgentaler decision. Under the previous provisions of the Criminal Code, by definition, every abortion performed in Canada was a medical procedure performed for a health rationale. For that reason funding was assured under the Canada Health Act.
I can remember that in my own province there were those who wished to pressure the provincial government not to fund abortion. They found that they could not because it was, by definition, a medical procedure under the Canada Health Act.
I believe that Bill C-43 accomplishes the same thing by its very clear definition of abortion being performed for a health rationale. Although that may disturb some people who are very much against abortion, I think they would agree that whatever the status of abortion in Canadian society, it ought to be a status that is uniform across the country. If it is to be a legal procedure, it ought to be equally accessible across the country, and I believe that Bill C-43, to the extent that the federal government has the jurisdiction to do so, accomplishes this.
Bill C-43 ensures that abortions will be carried out by or under the supervision of a qualified medical practitioner. Bill C-43 creates no barriers to access in the way of procedural requirements or the requirements that abortions must be performed in any specific facility, for example. Whether abortions performed in clinics will be funded under provincial medical plans is something that

November 21, 1989
Government Orders
is beyond the federal government to ensure, but abortions may be performed in a doctor's office or in a clinic without any legal penalty. The question of whether they will be funded under provincial plans is something that will have to be worked out with provincial governments. But, in so far as the federal government has jurisdiction, it has removed barriers to access that I think were very troublesome in the last bill.
I believe that Bill C-43 goes as far as federal jurisdiction can to ensure a national standard of access to safe, legal, funded abortions.
I would like to address some of the criticisms of Bill C-43 that have come from those who share my own position on the basic issue, criticisms from the prochoice side of the issue. Perhaps the most important criticism is with respect to this bill as an amendment to the Criminal Code and a distaste for what is described as the "recriminalization" of abortion.
I think there are two aspects of this. One is the concern that somehow women or doctors will be subject to arbitrary penalties for providing a medical service which many feel is a right that women should have in Canadian society. I think it is important to examine what is meant by recriminalization because what has been criminalized in this bill is, first, abortions performed by non-medical practitioners or not under the supervision of a medical practitioner; abortions performed without forming an opinion as to the health rationale which, as I said before, I believe is quite simply bad medical practice; and the sale of abortifacients, toxic devices or equipment to induce abortions or for women to induce abortions in themselves. Abortion is criminalized only in a very narrow sense.
What also offends many pro choice people with the notion of abortion being in the Criminal Code is that somehow they feel that having abortion mentioned in the Criminal Code implies a moral judgment even upon those who avail themselves of legal abortions. I think that is very much a misunderstanding of the way criminal law functions in our society. If you look through the Criminal Code at the subjects of things that are regulated under the Criminal Code you would find that many
perfectly acceptable kinds of activities in our society have been criminalized in certain contexts.
Those would include sexual intercourse, sexual touching, lighting a fire, gambling, being near a dwelling house at night, driving a car, possessing a narcotic, taking possession of property. Under certain circumstances those activities are all criminal and incur criminal penalties under the Criminal Code. But under other circumstances they are perfectly natural and acceptable activities in human society.
What this law does is draw a line around the legal practice of abortion and, beyond that line, certain practices relating to abortion will incur criminal penalties. But within that line activity is perfectly legal and there is no implied judgment upon those who avail themselves of the service, according to the law.
It is important to emphasize, as have my colleagues, that there is no other constitutional jurisdiction under which the federal government can act in this area. We do not have the constitutional jurisdiction to regulate health care. The residual jurisdiction of peace, order and good government is a very weak ground and unless we were to regard things happening about abortion as a national emergency, it is simply not a usable constitutional head of authority. So the only way the federal government can act at all to create some kind of national standard is to use its criminal law power. I think it is very important for people to understand that. The only way we can establish the legality of abortion in a positive legal statement is to define the boundaries beyond which it is illegal.
The question of access is the other aspect that is raised with respect to this bill. As I have said, there are limits to federal jurisdiction. I believe that the defined status of abortion as a medical procedure in this bill accomplishes a great deal toward ensuring equality of access across Canada. None of the barriers that existed under the old law, the committees, the need to perform abortions in accredited hospitals, exist in this legislation. I believe that this should ensure access for women in all parts of Canada.
The issue of abortion is, of course, something very fundamental to value systems in current Canadian society. It is impossible for us to have a legal framework
November 21, 1989

which will satisfy all. The Minister of Justice has said: "We are not asking Canadians to change their views as to what they think is right, we are asking Canadians to respect the views of others and to respect this new law."
That is a harder challenge than it first seems because I know how passionately I feel about my side of the issue, and I know that many of my colleagues feel equally passionate about their side of the issue. To give ground on that kind of a fundamental commitment is the most difficult thing you can ask of anyone. Tolerance is the hardest virtue to practice in a democratic society. For those of us who make laws, moving from highly principled positions is very difficult indeed.
What is interesting about this law is that it represents agreement on some aspects of the issue among people from both sides of the issue, although, interestingly enough, for different reasons. For example, my colleagues who are strongly anti- abortion are adamant, as my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has said, that abortion only be available for a health rationale. I can accept that because first, only a very broad definition of health will pass the House and will pass, I believe, court review. But also, from my perspective, a health rationale clarifies the status of abortion with respect to the Canada Health Act.
So, for very different reasons, we can agree on putting a health rationale into the bill. My colleagues who are strongly anti-abortion do not wish to see gestation limits in legislation. I agree with them on that but for different reasons. For them gestation limits suggest a varying value of human life at different times of pregnancy which is anathema to them. For me, gestation limits simply feed the myth in society that women seek abortions late in pregnancy when over 99 per cent of abortions are, in fact, sought in the first trimester of pregnancy.
You will remember that Chantal Daigle could not get an abortion in Quebec after 20 weeks. There was no law. There was no criminal law against abortion and there was no law in Quebec setting out gestational limits, but the ethics of the medical profession apply here. We sometimes forget that that is a very important force. That is a force recognized in this bill where decisions about abortions are made according to standard medical practice. There are substantive limitations within the Canadian Medical Association about the performance of
Government Orders
abortion. I and my colleagues who are on the other side of the issue can agree that it is not necessary or appropriate to have gestational limits in this bill. We have never had them in Canada. There are de facto gestational limits and they are gestational limits determined according to medical ethics in Canadian society.
The use of the criminal law is not only our only jurisdictional choice constitutionally, but I believe it also is a reflection on the seriousness of the issue. I had a letter recently from a very good friend of mine, a leader in the civil liberties field in Vancouver. He wrote to me congratulating the government on the bill. He is a person I admire very much because although he is deeply committed to civil liberties he is also a pragmatist who understands the difficulty of translating values into public policy. He says: " By retaining the criminality of the procedure the government has offered a potent symbol of conciliation to those veiy many Canadians who feel that this can never be seen or treated as just another moral issue. Its deep significance must, they insist, raise it to the level of the criminal law".
I think that recognition is appropriate. Strongly prochoice though I am, I recognize that abortion is not just another issue. It is a deeply important issue, it is a deeply important issue to me as a woman and all my understanding of what fertility means to a woman.
I would say in conclusion that I am among those Canadians who are comfortable with no law regulating abortion. I have confidence in the judgment of women and the ethics of the medical profession, and both of these views, I believe, are reflected in Bill C-43.
If this were all it would be a helpful declaration but not perhaps necessary. I do believe that Bill C-43 goes farther and, in clarifying the status of abortion as a medical procedure, it improves access. It also considerably narrows the range of possible legal challenges. I believe this law reflects the views of people on all sides of the issue although it does not reflect all the views of people on all sides of the issue.
The nature of the compromise that is required in this bill has been shown by the supporters of this bill. In reading some of the debate that has taken place so far and listening this evening, I am struck by the kind of maturity that is being shown in dealing with this very sensitive issue.

November 21, 1989
Government Orders
I believe that Canadians are looking to us to be pragmatic and to understand where the broad range of Canadians are. They are not asking us to give up our personal views or to cease our struggles in other arenas to convince others of our views. I believe that this bill is the best we can do and that it is an opportunity for us to show that we recognize the true role of parliamentarians in this House. For that reason, Madam Speaker, I am pleased to support the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was veiy interested to hear the rationale presented by the Minister who shares a pro-choice point of view. I want to raise two or three points that to me did not seem quite logical in her presentation. For one thing the Minister spoke about the medical aspect of the bill and felt this was a positive aspect of the bill. I wonder why she feels that it needs to be under the Criminal Code again when in fact abortion currently is a medical procedure and is regulated as a health matter.
She mentioned also in the Chantal Daigle case that the ethics of the medical profession applied in Quebec as far as the 20-week limit on abortions was concerned. Yet she was using the rationale that we need the Criminal Code in order to apply this at this time.
I would ask her why we need it when there was no need during that period when this was occurring in Quebec? I agree with her that there are health regulations in that the medical profession certainly has a code of ethics which is pretty general across Canada.
I am worried about the member's statement and the statement of a number of other government members on the question of equality of access. I cannot see how this bill provides for equality of access, including geographic access. I cannot see how it will help women in P.E.I. and Newfoundland who have no access to abortion now.
I certainly cannot see how it will encourage access in the future. I do not see how it will help those women who want an abortion, have made a decision, and do not have a valid health rationale. I think we have to agree with the difficulty this presents for many doctors who undoubtedly will feel that they have to interpret health with a fairly narrow rationale. These are women who do not, in honesty, have a health reason to seek an abortion, but who find it very difficult to be honest because they are desperate and this is their decision. I would ask her
to respond to those points. I find it very difficult to find them in her remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Let me respond first of all to the member's comment about gestational limits in the Criminal Code. I do not think the member understood what I said, or perhaps I did not express myself very well.
There are no gestational limits in this bill. We have never had legislated gestational limits for abortion in Canada. The point I was making is that I do not believe they are necessary. I believe that their existence in legislation reinforces a myth that I think is injurious to women and, therefore, I do not believe they should be in the legislation. In fact, they are not in the legislation. My colleagues on the other side of the issue from me also do not wish to have gestational limits.
In this bill there are some principles that we can agree on, although for different reasons. That is the point I was trying to make. My reason for not favouring gestational limits is different from the reasons that my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, would give. But the fact that we can agree on the substance of what should go in the bill is a step in the right direction. Therefore we have some consensus. The reasons are very different.
With respect to the member's question of access, her first and third questions, let me just draw on my own experience in British Columbia when the Morgantaler decision came out striking down provisions of the Criminal Code when there was no law. The government of British Columbia moved to restrict money for abortion, except in cases of rape and incest. That regulation was struck down, but it was struck down for a largely technical reason, that there was no statutory basis for it. But that could have been corrected by the legislature.
Where attempts to limit funding for abortion can be impugned as being veiled attempts to prevent abortion, I believe will not survive legal challenge. They will be seen as an attempt to invade the division of powers and invade the criminal field which is the sole jurisdiction of the federal government. I believe that without any law, it does leave the door open for the provinces, quite legitimately, to draw a distinction between abortions which are medically necessary and those which are not, and to fund only those which are medically necessary, drawing their own criteria. I believe this bill solves that problem by making it clear that every legal abortion in
November 21, 1989

Canada is a medical procedure performed for reasons of health.
When we get to the question of the valid health rationale and the breadth of it, we already have a fair amount of dicta in the jurisprudence of the Supreme Court of Canada, which indicates how health should be interpreted, which is why psychological health is included in this bill. A narrower definition, we believe, would not survive a constitutional challenge. I believe that health is a very broad concept. Chief Justice Dickson used the terminology, I believe, "the aspirations of a woman." There is other commentary. One thinks of the World Health Organization definition of health.
Under the previous legislation, the legislation that was struck down, there was strong pressure from pro-choice groups in Canada, that somewhere, somehow a definition of health, for the purposes of that provision of the Criminal Code, be defined as the World Health Organization definition. It was recognized that a broad definition of health would open up access to abortion.
I am the first to agree that putting that definition in the bill is the compromise, that having a health rationale is a compromise for somebody coming from my perspective. It is the provision that concerns strong pro-choice women. I believe that the definition is broad enough, and the trade-off in terms of securing the status of abortion, which I believe puts it firmly under the Canada Health Act, is a reasonable trade-off to make. I do not believe that that health rationale will be an impediment for any woman. I believe that it is important to see health in terms of the whole human being. The definition of this bill includes health as physical, mental or psychological which, it seems to me, those of us on the pro-choice side of the issue have been fighting for for years and fought for when we had to deal with the old law. We said there has to be a broad definition of health because otherwise the old law was not fair. The old law was struck down, but we are now faced with defining health in a helpful way.
So to answer the member's question about equality of access geographically, once again, I believe that in firmly putting abortion within the purview of the Canada Health Act, by removing the previous barriers, for example, the need to perform abortions in an accredited hospital which existed under the old legislation, the hurdle of therapeutic abortion committees without the
Government Orders
requirement to form them, that the federal government has done as far as is possible for it to do under its jurisdiction all it can to ensure access.
There is no legal penalty under this bill for a doctor to perform an abortion in Prince Edward Island. I believe that if provinces are not prepared to make those services available, that as with many other services that are not available in all jurisdictions in Canada, they will be obliged to provide funding for those services in other parts where they are available. There are many services for which this applies in Canadian health care.

Mr. Speaker, in the minister's speech she spoke about the role of the medical practitioner. It seemed to me she suggested that the medical practitioner's only role certainly was not the physical act of performing the abortion, but rather that it had to do with revolving around consent and that that consent should be based on information. The minister used the word "informed" consent.
Would the minister be willing to give a full and fair consideration to a potential amendment relating to informed consent? Second, might she consider an amendment that related to perhaps a period of time for reasoned judgment? In fact, after the first consultation with the medical practitioner there might be a 48-hour period whereupon further reflection and reasoned judgment could be brought to bear for that person to consider the information that the doctor, in fact, might give that woman. Third, would the minister define an abortion itself as the termination of life? Does the minister accept that definition, the termination of life is what an abortion is in fact?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the question of informed consent, no, I would not support that kind of amendment. First, there are already civil remedies against physicians for performing procedures where informed consent is absent. It is part of the law in Canada now with respect to medical procedure.
What I was speaking about was simply good medical practice-time for reasoned judgment. Once again, we are talking about this question of dealing with things in abstractions and trying to generalize about what are unique circumstances. One woman may come to a doctor and say, "I have been thinking about this now for two weeks, and I have talked to my clergyman, and I have talked to my partner, and I have talked to my parents, and I have been all around this issue and I have made

November 21, 1989
Government Orders
this decision and I just feel that I cannot go ahead with this pregnancy" for all these various reasons.
Another woman may come to her doctor in tears or simply may advise the doctor of her pregnancy and at that time begin the process of coming to a decision. I do not think it is the business of Parliament to dictate to practitioners how they deal with that. That is precisely the thing I fear, this desire to create a general regime for what is basically a unique situation for each person. I think we have to have some confidence in the medical profession. As I say, what I like about the way the health rationale is put in this bill is that it demands good medical practice for women in Canada.
Finally, the member asked me the question about whether abortion is the termination of life. That is a philosophical question. I do not accept the notion that a foetus has the same rights as a born human being. Maybe I am too much of a product of the common law, but I think that is an opinion and a discussion which is philosophical. We are trying to legislate in the real world and I do not think it is helpful to get into that discussion at this time.
