Mr. Speaker, I must say the Chair becomes you veiy well. I welcome this opportunity to participate in the debate on this bill and to put my views on the record with respect to the complex and difficult issue of abortion.
I wish to say that I have very carefully considered the views of the hundreds of my constituents who have taken the trouble to contact me either in person or by mail. I have also considered the many written materials sent to me by groups and organizations concerning this issue. I have told those who have contacted me that I take my responsibility in this matter very seriously.
I endeavour to approach this issue from what I would call a non-doctrinaire point of view. I seek to apply my judgment as a legislator trying to find a framework in law for the benefit of all Canadians.

Each and every one of us, as members of this House, must use his or her own judgment on this issue. As a group we bring a unique combiration mix of life experiences and of political and sometimes personal philosophies.

My own experience has been profoundly touched by the reality of life and death. I have witnessed the birth of each of my three children and these are three of the most precious moments of my life. At each of them and at the memory of them, I was and am moved by the miracle of human life.
My wife and I have also experienced the grief of a miscarriage and we have shared in difficult decisions relating to the use of artificial life support for both of my parents.
The need to reflect on matters of birth, life and death can escape none of us for these are the common denominators of the human experience. Consideration of matters of life and death is not limited to abortion. Modern technology presents us with a host of questions about life and death that never before needed to be answered by humankind. Some of these questions, in vitro fertilization, surrogate parenthood, voluntary euthanasia, create difficulties that are as profound as those presented by abortion.
I believe the principle that life is special is self-evident and even that it is not in dispute, including in this debate. Some refer to this principle as the sanctity of life. Human life should represent in a civilized society a very special value, a higher value. Human life itself should be preserved and protected as the highest possible priority of human endeavour and ingenuity.
Life, however, is much broader than the issue before us. Human life itself cannot exist independent of other life forms on this planet. What we must be learning from the environmental crises that surround us is surely this:
November 21, 1989

While human life may be sanctified, it will only be preserved on this planet if we show concern and respect for our world, its plant and animal life forms as well.

Have we not finally understood that all life forms are interdependent? Respect for life involves a lot more than just preventing abortions.

That being said, it also seems to me to be self-evident that human life begins before birth. Nature in its own course provides for the human child to be carried by its mother well beyond the point at which modern technology has rendered it viable outside the mother.
I also believe in the principle that in our society, the maximum possible scope for individual freedom or choice should be permitted. I do believe, however, that freedom to choose brings with it the obligation to accept the consequences of one's choices. We take pride, and rightly so, in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms but sometimes I believe that we should have a charter of rights and obligations because obligations flow necessarily from rights.
I am not unaware of, nor do I disregard, the views of those who believe that a woman should have the right to control her own body. I am not one who favours a pervasive government interference in the private lives of individuals and I believe that matters of private morality should not be within the purview of the state.
I have heard the plea from some women that the life within a pregnant woman, especially in the early stages of pregnancy, is not independent life but really part and parcel of her own body. To enact a criminal law to interfere with a woman's control over this aspect of her person is viewed as a profound interference in a woman's private, personal matters.
I understand this viewpoint and I am responsive to it, especially to the extent that I believe that the state should have less rather than more control over the personal lives of individuals. But I find enormous difficulty with the view that the unborn child, especially after the point of viability, has no right to protection by the state.
Government Orders
Having outlined my view of the meaning of respect for life and the need to accept responsibility for one's choices, I would like to comment on the proper role of the criminal law in this matter.
First of all, as a lawyer, I agree that the sole head of federal jurisdiction in this matter is the criminal law power, whether exercised through the Criminal Code or otherwise. This requires us to define an offence and to prescribe a penalty.
I also believe that the rule of law is fundamental to our system of government. Without the rule of law, that is, the acceptance that the law is paramount and of equal application to all, the integrity of our system of government will be undermined. The acceptance of the rule of law depends upon respect for the laws we enact in this place, fortunately, far more than it depends upon respect for us as legislators. The importance of this principle should give legislators great pause in deciding to enact a criminal law.
What is required for us to enact a criminal law to prohibit behaviour in our society? I believe that a very broad consensus within our society is required, a consensus which encompasses the following elements: First of all, the behaviour which is prohibited is such that it should be punished. The behaviour must offend against society's view of acceptable behaviour. Second, the person to be punished for committing the offence must be deserving of punishment. Third, the punishment must be fair and reasonable in the circumstances.
I have been told by some of those who support a law prohibiting abortion that it does not matter if the law cannot be enforced or if it is commonly disobeyed. It is enough for them that the law be in place to demonstrate society's values even if enforcement is impossible, impracticable or even undesirable. On the latter point, some have told me that they favour an abortion law but would not like to see women punished for disobeying it. These statements undermine for me the argument for legal intervention.

I suggest that if the law is not enforced or is full of loopholes or if juries refuse to convict those who disobey it, there will be us respect for the law and this will thus undermine the Canadian legal system.

Government Orders

There are doubtless many times that citizens consider the law to be an ass, as Mr. Bumble said in Oliver Twist, but when this is said of the criminal law in respect of a matter which touches people broadly in the country, the danger to respect for law is intensified.
The values implicitly or explicitly contained in the submissions I have received, both in favour of and opposed to a law, are not reconcilable, premised as they are on a fundamentally different view of the time at which human life begins and is worthy of protection.
I must say that some of the extreme presentations of these points of view have been rather offensive to me. This debate, more than most, has resulted in the characterization of opposing views in provocative and extreme epithets reflecting to the disgrace of those who make them.
I too am a product of my upbringing, my experience of life, my legal training and, perhaps most important, my faith and the understanding it gives me of life and the meaning of the universe. The views that I hold of matters of life and death are the ones that I will teach my children and that I will seek to apply in my personal life. But as a legislator, I am responsible for shaping laws that will affect the rights of other people in matters of life and death. In our pluralistic society, I cannot expect that everyone will agree with my views or accept my values. But a society must have values which it owns and which unite it. It is to these values that I now appeal.
The first, as I have explained, is the principle that the laws we enact must be worthy of and receive the respect of the population. But further, I believe that we share values in Canada that will provide us with the affirmation of human life that is sought by caring people. It is upon these values that we have built a system of social programs that is envied by other nations.
As Governor Mario Cuomo of New York has said:
We should understand that whether abortion is outlawed or not, our work has barely begun: the work of creating a society where the right to life doesn't end at the moment of birth; where an infant isn't helped into a world that doesn't care if it's fed properly, housed decently,
educated adequately; where the blind or retarded child isn't condemned to exist rather than empowered to live.
The unfortunate truth is that in Canada, abortion is often motivated by economic considerations. If we condemn some of our people to live in poverty, whether through lack of jobs, lack of adequate child care or an unfair tax system, can we rightly criticize these same people when they seek to mitigate their responsibilities? If we keep our young people in ignorance, if we deny them the moral guidance and the physical means to avoid unwanted pregnancy, is it fair to condemn them when they seek the means to continue their adolescence without the interruption and responsibility that childbirth provides?
If I have never experienced rape or incest, how can I judge whether a woman impregnated in these circumstances is wrong to want to remove from within her the consequences of these violations of her person and her dignity? Again, quoting Governor Cuomo:
If we want to prove our regard for life in the womb, for the helpless infant-if we care about women having real choices in their lives and not being driven to abortions by a sense of helplessness and despair about the future of their child-then there is work enough for all of us. Lifetimes of it.
We must see that justice is done, not only for the unborn, but also for their parents. Any abortion law should be accompanied by a very positive pro-active agenda that will endeavour to prevent unwanted pregnancy, to support mothers during pregnancy, to enable families to live without hardship and to ensure that women have readily available to them counselling services and advice concerning the adoption alternative and to ensure that no woman obtains an abortion who might have been willing and able to bear a living child.
As Canadians, let us find common ground for policies and programs based on these values, values which affirm the dignity of human life, values that promote caring and compassion.
Before I conclude, I wish to comment specifically on Bill C-43. During the election campaign and since, I have maintained that I would support a law that would protect the unborn and that would be consistent with the Charter of Rights. I believe that Bill C-43 meets or appears to meet the minimum requirements of this test.
I have carefully reviewed once more the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Morgentaler and I believe as a lawyer that the proposed bill is constitution-
November 21, 1989

al. However, I do not disagree with the suggestion that the bill be tested by reference to the court after enactment but before proclamation.
However, I believe this bill to be fundamentally dishonest. It appears to protect the unborn from the time of conception, and yet it is hard to see how even one abortion would be prevented under this law. It appears to leave the matter to a woman and her doctor to decide and yet it criminalizes the act of abortion and I believe exposes doctors to real peril of prosecution.
In short, I fail to see how this bill can do other than to lead to disrespect for law. Would Canada have an abortion law? Yes. But that law would be worse than a bad law or no law. That law would be a joke.
Because of the critical importance of respect for law to the rule of law and of the rule of law for the preservation of freedom, I cannot support this bill. I will not vote for a law that will fuel cynicism and contribute to a sense that the laws we enact here, much like the talk we often engage in, are irrelevant to contemporary society.
I will vote for the bill on second reading, however, not because I support it in principle, but because I think the matter should be studied by a committee of this House and amendments considered. I will vote against this bill in its present form at third reading.
For the record, I will say that I absolutely support the use of criminal law to prohibit abortion after the foetus is viable as an independent human life. It is to me totally unacceptable for an abortion to take place after the point of viability which I understand may be as early as 21 weeks. How can we countenance an abortion in one hospital room of a foetus at the same stage of development as that of a premature baby whose life we are seeking to save in a room just down the corridor? Only if it is a matter of saving the mother's life should the life of a viable foetus be sacrificed. I believe most Canadians agree with this, and would support such a law.
In the earlier stages of pregnancy, I am not any more content that abortions occur, but I draw back from the prohibition of elective abortion at an early stage, not because I think the unborn has any less value at 12 weeks
Government Orders
than at 20 or 30 weeks, but because I perceive that such a prohibition would not be enforceable.
I am offended by the reality that abortion is being used in Canada as a means of birth control in 1989. There can be no other explanation for the number of abortions that occur in Canada each year. It is evident that in many of these cases, choice is exercised irresponsibly before conception and abortion is the means of avoiding the consequences of one's choice.
However, I believe society does not accept that the state should intervene in the life of an individual woman at this stage of pregnancy. I also believe that if the state attempts to do so, the result will be legal chaos, with confrontations between police and groups, refusals by juries to convict accused, and also, unfortunately, many illegal abortions and the gruesome possibility of back alley and self-inflicted abortions.
Whatever my own opinion about whether abortion is right or wrong, I cannot as a legislator support the enactment of such a law, one which will not be effective and could cause hardship and suffering for those whose act is viewed by society as essentially private and unworthy of attention by the state.
I feel the burden of this legislative responsibility to be very heavy. I know that many will criticize me for the conclusion I have reached since, like Bill C-43 itself, it satisfies neither extreme in this debate.
In response, I say two things: First, I do not believe that we are here to debate whether abortion is good or bad, right or wrong. Rather, we must debate and decide what is the best legislative response within the constitutional powers of the Parliament of Canada to the issue resulting from the demand from women to obtain abortions. Second, my response is to remember the advice given by Polonius to his son in Hamlet:
This above all, lo thine own self be true.
And it must follow as the night the day
thou canst not then be false to any man.

Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by briefly outlining my position in support of the protection of the life of the foetus or the unborn child. First, it is well known that all of the components necessary for the development of a unique individual human being are contained in the genetic code

November 21, 1989
Government Orders
that is present from the moment of conception, the hue of our eyes, the colour of our hair, the size of our feet, as well as the capacity of our brains, have all been established in that instant. Nothing needs to be added, other than food, shelter and care.
Second, the indicators of life and its development are manifested early and dramatically. The unborn child produces its own blood at 17 to 20 days after conception. Its heart begins beating from 20 to 24 days after conception. Between the sixth and seventh weeks, the electrical activity of the brain is discernible and at the eighth week, all essential organs are present.
Canada has accepted in medical practice that the cessation of brain wave activity is the irreversible indicator of death. Well then, should it not be reasoned that the first readable signs of brain wave activity confirm the presence of life? Nevertheless, our behaviour as a society deliberately and in a premeditated manner destroys that life. From Statistics Canada's figures for 1986 and 1987, it can be readily seen that approximately 75 per cent of all abortions occur after the beginning of brain wave activity.
I think it is highly instructive to read how, in 1975, after an exhaustive examination of the available biological and physiological evidence by 133 world-renowned scientists, geneticists and gynaecologists, the West German Federal Constitutional Court responded to the question as to when life begins. It is also important to note that the court was acutely conscious of the historical events which took place between 1933 and 1945, and was therefore especially anxious to ground its judgment in scientific objectivity. Its conclusion was:
Life, in the sense of historical existence of a human individual, exists according to definite biological-physiological knowledge, in any case, from the 14th day after conception -
Or the period of nidation or individuation.
The process of development which has begun at that point is a continuing process which exhibits no sharp demarcation and does not allow a precise division of the various steps of development of the human life.
In view of this concrete evidence, it is a sad commentary on our society that one's position on abortion can then be construed, and thereby dismissed by some, as being simply a matter of personal opinion or belief. No,
it is not a matter of personal opinion; the medical evidence of life is concrete, it is objective, it is compelling. To anyone with an open, enquiring and honest mind, life then must be accepted as an uninterrupted continuum which begins at conception and ends at death. Without doubt, abortion brings about the death of a living human individual during the process of its development along that continuum.
I fail to see why anyone including our Supreme Court Justices, do not see this logic, for surely a human foetus will never result in a cat, dog or a horse but only in a human being which it became at conception and will remain so until death. Only shelter, food and normal development and protection is required throughout pregnancy or up to age two, or five, or fifteen, or twenty, or fifty, or seventy years of age.
Dr. Jerome Lejeune, one of the world's foremost human geneticists, stated the following to the United States Senate Committee in 1983:
-if a fertilized egg is not by itself a full human being, it could never become a man, because something would have to be added to it, and we know that that does not happen.
After I read the tortured reasoning of the Supreme Court Justices which they revealed in their judgment of November 16, 1989, in the Chantal Daigle case, I wished and I prayed that someone could get our judges to contemplate the simple yet profound common sense of what Dr. Lejeune said.
Indeed, according to Sir William Lilley of New Zealand, knighted because of his pioneering work in amniocentesis, the unborn child is not a part of the mother's body, as some incorrectly suggest, but rather is a separate person who dictates his or her own growth and when he or she is to be bom. Therefore, it is absolutely essential that our laws protect life from conception. That is why it is so important that the government reject any legislative proposal that followed the gestational or highly arbitrary approach of foetal viability.
The bill before us implicitly recognizes that life begins at conception by placing a criminal sanction against the taking of foetal life. Further, the criminal prohibition on abortion is throughout the pregnancy and is not only mandatory to protect the sanctity of life but also this criminal sanction is highly symbolic. Mr. Joseph Main-got, a member of the Law Reform Commission which
November 21, 1989

issued a paper this past summer entitled "Crimes Against the Foetus", put this very well when he stated:
The criminal law is our nation's fundamental statement of public policy. It is the instrument by which the community draws a line between the tolerable and the intolerable. Criminal law defines those whose interests are worthy of respect and protection, and in my view this should include all members of the human family. Ultimately the criminal law is a mirror of what we are; it reflects our commitment, or lack of commitment, to human dignity and equality.
The law does not exist for the sole or primary purpose of punishing illicit acts. It exists as an expression, in a broad sense, of the kind of people we are. It does not merely regulate our behaviour, it articulates and symbolizes our values and beliefs.
I am pleased that the government heeded this advice and demonstrated its respect for human life and made the taking of a life by abortion a crime within the Criminal Code except under certain circumstances. This action by the government is in keeping with the invitation of our Supreme Court in its decision on the Morgentaler case of January 28, 1988, in which Chief Justice Dickson wrote:
The precise point in the development of the foetus at which the state's interest in its protection becomes 'compelling' should be left to the informed judgment of the legislature.
In this bill, the government has defined that precise point as conception when the state interest should become compelling since the criminal sanction against taking foetal life applies from conception. The Supreme Court decision of Januaiy 28, 1988, also stated in the judgment of Chief Justice Dickson:
Like Beetz and Wilson, I agree that the protection of foetal interests by Parliament is also a valid governmental objective. It follows that balancing these interests with the lives and health of women a major factor, is clearly an important governmental objective.
This balancing of interests between that of the mother and her unborn child is also a part of the bill before us in that it allows an abortion only when the life or health of the female person is likely to be threatened. If we in this House believe in the sanctity of life, we must ensure that there is an equal concern for the well-being of both mother and child.
Unfortunately, the abortion debate has been interpreted by some as being one of competing interests; the right of the mother to be free to choose versus the right of her unborn child to live. However, it surely defies all that we hold dear about humanity to speak of a mother
Government Orders
and her unborn child as being in competition against one another. Only a pathetically distorted sense of what is right, or what is freedom of choice, or what is demanded as control over my own body, or what is a deliberate act of ignoring all medical and scientific evidence could render a mother and her child as antagonists.
In view of the limitations placed upon us by the Charter of Rights, I would like to state the following: I believe an abortion should be performed only on the grounds of self defence in those very limited number of circumstances where the mother's life and narrowly defined health is, in the opinion of a medical doctor, in demonstrable danger, and where there is no other accepted medical procedure to treat that danger according to the opinion formed using, as this bill says: "the generally accepted standards of the medical profession."
I would submit that this bill is sound in principle. Life from conception must be protected within our Criminal Code. It is also on the right track in that it permits an abortion only when there is a threat to the mother. But the bill goes far beyond that by permitting an abortion, not only for the rare legitimate reasons of the life of the mother but for health broadly defined as physical, mental, and psychological.
That definition of health is so broad, so open to abuse, that abortion could be and has been justified by unscrupulous and unprincipled doctors for almost any reason. Anyone who has studied the reasons for abortions from 1969 to January 1988 knows full well that veiy few abortions were performed, one, to save the mother's life or, two, to save the mother's physical well-being where in the professional opinion of the doctors involved there was no other medical procedure or option to treat that risk. In fact, Madam Speaker, the vast majority of abortions were performed for reasons of convenience and the desire simply not to have the child.
Therefore, this bill is in obvious need of, in fact it cries out for, amendments to circumscribe more definitive boundaries and standards around the word "health" so that we truly are balancing the interests involved.
We need to carefully consider adding words such as "seriously endangering" the pregnant woman's health. Further, we need to clearly state that an abortion should be only undertaken by a doctor if in his professional opinion there is no other medical procedure or option

November 21, 1989
Government Orders
open to him to treat this serious health risk endangering the pregnant woman.
I also think we must strike out the word "psychological" in the definition of health and retain the words "physical and mental", but only within the constraints I have just mentioned. I think the bill should demand, and I also take it as a given, that every doctor would retain a written documentation of his professional medical judgment justifying the performance of the abortion.
We must carefully consider other amendments such as Mr. Justice Beetz indicated when he wrote:
Parliament is justified in requiring a reliable, independent and medically sound opinion in order to protect the state interest in the foetus.
Further he stated:
Parliament requires this independent opinion because it is not only the woman's interest that is at stake in a decision to authorize an abortion".
The penalty against unlawful abortion proposed in this bill is that it is an indictable offence with a possible prison term not exceeding two years. If the principle of the bill is to protect life and to balance both the interests of mother and child, then surely two years is woefully inadequate and an amendment providing a term of up to 15 years or life is far more appropriate. Only then would we be truly protecting life as we do in manslaughter or murder cases.
The purpose of second reading debate is to debate the principle of the bill. I believe that one of the principles of the bill is to protect the life of the foetus or the unborn child from conception. This bill does this by placing a criminal sanction against the taking of that life from conception.
The bill also seeks to balance the vital interests of both the mother's and child's life by permitting an abortion only when the life or health of the mother is likely to be threatened. In this case, the bill is far too weak to achieve any proper balance by not carefully limiting the word "health", by providing only up to a possible two-year prison sentence and not requiring an independent medical opinion.
The way the bill now stands, all of its provisions are on the side of the mother and next to nothing protects the child within her womb. To succinctly summarize the nature of this bill, I would submit that one could
characterize this bill as one that is pro-life in form and pro-choice in substance. It is pro-life in that it assumes that life begins at conception and should be protected throughout the pregnancy. But it is pro-choice in that it literally permits a woman to go to any doctor prepared to do abortions simply for cases of anxiety or alleged psychological harm.
Nevertheless, because at least the basic principle of protecting the unborn from conception is the implicit foundation of the bill, I will support it at second reading in spite of its serious inadequacies which I will seek to amend at committee and report stages when amendments are permissible. I do not support this bill with any joy within my heart. I do so only after much soul searching and only in order to make full use of all of the opportunities the process affords us as members of this House to make amendments to improve this bill so that the vast majority of abortions done for none other than the frivolous and shameful reasons of convenience might decrease in number. Then and only then will we begin to do what we in this chamber should always strive toward, to defend the innocent, the weak and the powerless and to stand for the truth and for the protection of the sanctity of life that that truth demands of each of us.

Madam, Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in this important debate, a sometimes very moving debate. We have had experiences with that here tonight. A very sincere group of speakers has been addressing the problem with which we are all wrestling with.
I am sure we all bring different perspectives to the debate. The perspectives are as varied as are the people addressing the bill. I personally bring all of my life experiences to what I am about to say. My sense of worth and my sense of values are going to be brought into the discussion as I am sure will those of many who will address the bill. In spite though of all these variances that we find among ourselves, we would all agree on some fundamentals I think, one of these basic fundamentals being that life is worth while, life is a valuable entity, life is worth protecting.
I am sure that to argue otherwise would contradict what we see going on in any hospital in the city of Ottawa tonight. Doctors and nurses are there working to try and
November 21, 1989

preserve a life. Lifelong sacrifices are being made by some families to preserve a life, a life which some would have thought was not worth preserving. There is something very, very fundamental that touches us all when we talk about preserving life. It does not matter whether it is a big person or a small person, a young person or an old person, a sick person or one who is well. All people are very different. All are lives and in spite of different surroundings, in spite of totally different circumstances, they are worth our protection.
That is what this debate is all about. Sometimes we get off on ramifications of economics and so on and I have heard it mentioned here tonight. It seems to suggest that economics should be the dividing line. We are talking about life, fundamental life.
Our obligation as human beings is to protect the lives of others who are in no position to do so. They have no voice. A tremendous moral responsibility rests upon us to particularly protect those who cannot protect themselves. The inconvenience that one life may cause to another life is not justification for the dominant one to discontinue the life of the innocent one. In no way is that justification to turn somebody else's life around, to discontinue the life of that person because somebody happens to be in a stronger position.
A child on the verge of being bom is developmentally indistinguishable from a newborn infant. In a free and democratic society infants have the status of persons. They possess fundamental rights, including the right to life and the right to legal protection.
The mere fact that a baby is inside someone else's body does not imply to me that it is not a person. If it is not a person at this stage, presumably the reason for that is that it is still physically dependent on its mother. But if its personhood is diminished in this way by dependence then the personhood of seriously ill people who are on life support systems would come into question as would the personhood of other seriously dependent or handicapped persons with whom we are surrounded daily.
If intrinsic value of the life were diminished by dependence, some persons would have less intrinsic value than others, and I think that would bring our Charter of Rights with regard to life into play. The
Government Orders
problem I have with viability as a determinant is that the level of development at which the foetus becomes viable depends on the stage of medical science and technology. We have made tremendous strides in society in that area of science in recent years. Let us not turn our back on it.
I think it would be a disgrace, a reflection on the personhood of people to turn our back on newly developed medical techniques and newly developed awareness such as we have heard spoken of here tonight, things which we did not know 25, 50, 75 years ago. I do not think we should turn our back on new medical evidence that life begins at conception.
Section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms says: "Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right of the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination".
Failure to protect the life of the foetus by law would, in my opinion, be permitting the taking of a life. If a law prohibiting infant abuse becomes unenforceable, or very difficult to enforce because of widespread deterioration in values in our society, that would not be sufficient reason to promote the absence of such a law. It is difficult to enforce but surely we do that in society all the time.
If no one's life is valuable enough to protect by law then none of us really have any basic rights. If a foetus has the right to have its life protected by law, such a law is justifiable in a free and democratic society and it is in accordance with our Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
On January 28, 1988, the Supreme Court of Canada declared Canada's abortion law unconstitutional. We need a new law which will be found to be constitutional. Certain women's groups, and I have heard this alluded to here today, oppose any form of protection for the foetus. I want to caution women. The justice women which have achieved, and rightly so, will be seriously undermined in society if it is bought at the price of injustice to persons conceived but not yet bom. Women will lose. If they think that gives them the right to impose upon and extinguish the rights of others, what have they gained? There is tremendous risk if women feel that they now have the right to impose their new found rights, justifiably distinguished and determined, for which I give them all sorts of credit, but not pushing it so far that they think

November 21, 1989
Government Orders
they can now impose rights on others who are in no position to express themselves.
Pregnancy concerns the whole person. It concerns the family, it concerns the community, and I think it concerns all of society. It requires, above all, communities and a society that cares. It is like poverty, which is a concern of all society. Racial inequality is a concern of all society. Institutionalized abortion means to me that the community is opting out, opting out of caring; caring socially, caring economically, caring judicially and caring personally.
To say that a man, the male species, should not comment on abortion because it is something that he will never experience is a simple way of copping out too. I have never witnessed war. I have never been on the front lines of war. I have read much about it and have heard many stories about it, but surely I can have some appreciation for that. I have some appreciation of what war must be like. I feel confident and certain that I can speak out on that issue and try to see that we will never have that to contend with again, although I have not experienced it myself.
If we have legislation to protect the unborn, I think the state then has a responsibility to introduce social programs which will assist people for whom abortion seems to present the only temporaiy solution to their problems. There is some responsibility for the state here which includes such programs as access to counselling; the full range of adoption options explained to people; housing needs, on which the determination to have an abortion is very often made; the provision of time for parenting and child care; programs in child care; affirmative action for fathering, something which probably was not thought of a few years back but should be addressed in today's changing times. Above all, we need education to prevent unwanted pregnancies.
Calling anything a woman's issue strikes me, personally, as being rather offensive. Spouse beating, day care and abortion are society's issues, they are not strictly and rigidly women's issues. It would be like calling apartheid a South African issue. Apartheid is not a South African issue, it is a universal society issue and society is no one gender, race, colour or religion. Injustices of the past toward women or any other group in society cannot be
corrected by perpetuating further injustices and denying life to unborn children.
I am asking my hon. friends who have not thought this through or have not taken a position to consider voting for the life of the unborn. Come down on the side of human dignity, be a promoter of life. What legitimate right requires for the exercise of that right the infliction of pain and death on another innocent human life? I ask that question.
There are two lives here to consider and, therefore, the moral question of abortion is absolutely not a women's rights issue exclusively. It involves the question of whether it is moral to dispose of or to destroy the weaker of the two individuals. When two people enter one of Morgentaler's clinics, only one comes out.
History tells us that in more barbaric times if a woman condemned to die was found to be pregnant, the execution was postponed to allow the innocent party to be born. In pregnancy there are two different heartbeats, two different brain wave patterns, often two different blood types and, in about half the cases, two different sexes. There are two people involved.
The question is not so much should they break the law but rather should they kill babies? That is the question. In a civilized society one does not kill one human being to alleviate the problems of another human being. We would not tolerate that. This bill would allow that to happen.
The foetus is not just a potential human being but rather, in my opinion, a human being with full potential that needs time to develop and to mature. Life is a continuum. It is not measured in weeks, in inches, in pounds or in kilograms, life is a continuum.
I do not think it is good enough to say that the legislation will be okay because most people's rights are respected. We are talking about individual rights. An apology to those whose most basic right, that of life, has been denied does no good whatsoever. As long as just one person's rights are encorached upon with the result that life is denied them, then I think society is in deep trouble.
I heard tonight that every child is a wanted child. That suggests great love, a reaching out for children. It is a common slogan, but let me remind you, Madam Speaker, that this slogan is not quite as loving as it sounds. It reduces children to objects with the right to exist only if
November 21, 1989

somebody wants them more than some other material thing. I think life is worth more than that.
Abortion is an attempt to solve one's personal problems by eliminating the life of another. Nothing threatens the most basic foundation of human civilization more directly than the widespread assault on the sanctity of life, whether it is by terrorists, plain murderers, or by the advocates of unrestricted abortion and euthanasia. Such cheapening of human life, apart from destroying the highest moral values, cannot but encourage the rise of crime and violence in our society. It is part of the throw-away society. Already crime is inflicting humanity at an alarming scale.
Any solution that I would have to this topic we are discussing would not be without any problems either. I admit that. I concede that. But we solve a problem because it is there and it challenges us. We have a problem confronting the Parliament of Canada now.
How terrible it would be if someone levelled all the mountains in life and, if it were possible, removed all the problems that we will be confronted with over our lifespan. There would not be any opportunity left for human beings to become really human, with the real qualities of a human being, if there were no challenges left.
What better time in the history of this country to show some leadership and be viewed by the rest of the world as the most generous, the most compassionate people in the world and the nation which showed the most human dignity in the world. All of us are here because of the generosity and the sacrifice of someone else. I think we have an obligation to others to return that sacrifice that others made on our behalf.
The gestational approach which has been mentioned tonight is unacceptable in principle because I think it arbitrarily determines that human life is more worthy of respect at some stages than at others and this, it seems to me, lends itself to selective living and selective dying. To offer easy access to abortion shows a callous failure of responsibility to protect life. To outlaw it, on the other hand, without proposing some positive measures to remedy the situations that we have heard mentioned here tonight encountered by pregnant women would also amount to a failure of responsibility.

I am suggesting a coherent and effective family life policy. It would require a co-ordinated effort from all levels of government.
Instead of this proposed legislation, which is just a fancy way of having abortion on demand, I think the government should be proposing a family life plan which could then be supported by all members because it is something positive. It is a positive attitude toward life. Measures would have to be taken in education, labour, revenue, and housing, as has been mentioned.
In closing, what I am asking is a new approach to something that is very old. If you take away life as a basic right, all other rights that you would extend to the foetus are meaningless. Do without that one, you will do without them all.
Why not reject this proposed law in favour of a family life policy that is positive toward life in its outlook, one that would see the family elevated above every other social unit or organization-the ultimate unit, the family, the one that is of prime importance if we are to advance as a society on the world scene.
I think Canada has an opportunity to show leadership. Forget about party differences. What I am proposing is developing an attitude that respects the family and transcends all the petty differences we find when we bring party lines into play.
I think we must commit ourselves to elevating our purposes once and for all. Do something because it is right although it may not be popular. Do it because it is right.

Madam Speaker, I will not be supporting this bill. I am tom terribly on it. At the present time I do not think you will ever reach ideals unless you are prepared to pursue those ideals. To break it off and say "I can support it, although I do not quite support it on something as basic as human life" puts me in a bit of a jam.
I am really puzzled at the people who normally would be here at my left, and I do not want to get into great debate with them. These are supposed to be the people who have great compassion for people. They are not showing too much compassion when it comes to this little person who cannot defend himself. Madam Speaker, I have listened with great attention to the hon. member. I think that much of this debate tonight has been very thoughtful, and many of his comments fall into that category. I am struggling to give him the kind of respect that I think is accorded to those who participate in this debate.
However, when he makes comments that women choose to have an abortion because it is part of a throw-away society, for some material thing, as a woman I take great umbrage.
This is the kind of attitude that causes women to want to make it very clear that this is a woman's issue. I would like him to comment on that.

It is a woman's issue, but because women are part of society, it is a societal issue. I do not think it is strictly and solely a woman's issue.
My basic premise is that there are two people involved. If you do not agree with that, then of course you disagree with what I have said. If you do not agree with that, that there are two people involved, then I can see where you take the position that you have already taken.
It is a woman's issue. Because women as men and children and everyone else are part of society, it is a societal issue. It is something as fundamental as life. It is a societal issue.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the hon. member opposite, the Member for Leeds-Grenville. Certainly I would not try to influence him, and it is basic in my view that he asks to some extent that the House not play politics on such a basic and important matter. For quite some time I have been working on the pro-life side of the question, and I am proud of it. What I do not understand is the position taken by the hon. member opposite. As it seems to me after examining and pondering the legislation, it protects the fetus to a much larger extent more than I have heard him state. So much so Madam Speaker, that it recognizes it not as an extension but rather as a part of the human being, because it introduces the concept of criminal act into the thought process and the legislation. Again, I would not try to influence the hon. member, but it seems to me he could reflect a moment on that double dimension and his personal position, which I share indeed.

I have difficulty agreeing with you if, as I understood you to say, this bill protects the foetus. This bill allows open season on the foetus. All you have to do is convince a doctor that you have some physical ailment-it could be a scratchy throat or a headache that you did not used to have that-and attribute it then to your pregnancy.
I am thinking of certain doctors, and I will not mention names, who do not have much guiding them, it seems to me, morally. They would have no trouble accepting your word for that and perhaps getting a signature or whatever is required of them to give to you so that you could have your pregnancy terminated. I do not see much in
November 21, 1989

the bill that would prevent that from happening. Indeed,
I think it will become commonplace.
The next thing that follows of course in a country that gets too liberal on abortion policy is to permit euthanasia. I think China is a good example of that. I was reading in the newspaper the other day that China has a very liberal abortion policy. Right now in China euthanasia can be performed in hospitals. The state does not interfere. Somebody in the hospital decides that somebody's life should be snuffed out. It is permitted in China today without question.
I think you will be finding yourselves with this kind of legislation which is so weak in terms of protection of the foetus.
To me, it permits abortion on demand. If it is not on demand immediately the legislation passes, then the tendency with any legislation like this, though, is to become more and more liberal as society becomes more and more accepting of it. If it is not abortion on demand immediately, it soon will be. I am going back to what has happened in China where they went with a very liberal abortion policy and now they have euthanasia wholesale.

Madam Speaker, never in the Canadian parliamentary history have elected representatives been confronted with such an agonizing issue as that of legislating abortion.
During this last year especially, so much has been said and repeated on the subject, so many arguments have been put forward in support of legalizing or prohibiting it; so many extreme, intolerant, not to say disquieting reactions have come from legal, health and other professionals, people in responsible positions; there has been such an escalation in the media sometimes bordering on indecency, that I wonder if there is any point today to preach one way or the other.
Maximum exploitation of the victims of situations that arose last year has helped radicalize the already irreconcilable positions of both sides of the question. What with publicity, the temperature kept rising, and verbal violence even erupted at times. Is it any surprise that our fellow citizens differ in their views when the interpreta-
Government Orders
tion of government actions varies from one newspaper to the other? Indeed, after our legislation was tabled, we could read on November 4 in the Edmonton Journal: "This Bill makes sense"; in the Ottawa Citizen, "Abortion compromise pleases no one"; in the Gazette: "MPs on both sides unhappy with"; in Le Devoir. "Ottawa recriminalise l'avortement"; finally, in La Presse: "La femme et son medecin decideront de Vavortement''.
Madam Speaker, first of all, I want to make quite clear that I am neither a lawyer, a doctor nor a social worker. I am a citizen of this country, a mother and a grandmother, and my hair is white. However, I am very much aware of the debate that is going on today, in and outside Parliament and before our highest courts. I am also very aware of the many comments I have read and heard, of often hasty judgments that would benefit from a more critical view, and the many personal statements that at times I found chilling. And here I am again, in the same situation we had during the debate in 1988, tom between my personal convictions as a woman, as a Christian and a Catholic. I also have my responsibilities as a legislator, and I am a member of a government that is seeking legislation that is in line with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, while it is also seeking the best solution, and does so in the best interests of the society it has been asked to lead. The government and Parliament cannot and must not claim to dictate to women what they can think and do.
The government's role is to help these women opt for life, for having a child and a family. It is not the State's role to act as their conscience and to make for them a choice that is so difficult and problematic.
Last summer, journalist Jean-Luc Mongrain wrote the following in the heat of the debate, and I quote:
We don't need full-page ads of guilt messages. When we have to make decisions as important, as intimate, as disturbing and as profoundly existential as these, we certainly do not want to be hustled by people defending the ideololgies of pro-life or prochoice!
We need people who listen and understand, who reach out and are tolerant, and we need love and understanding. No court and no Parliament will ever be able to satisfy us and provide the right answer.
Experience has taught me the following: Coercive laws will not change people's attitudes. To try to understand the human drama going on today, we need tolerance and

November 21, 1989
Government Orders
an open mind. In most cases, the problem we are discussing today is a disturbing reality for those who are directly involved.
Following a judgment by the Supreme Court on abortion, some people shouted and screamed that the so-called legal vacuum had to be filled as soon as possible.
The opposition in Parliament, many editorial writers, those whose only defence and opinion is to pass the buck-all these people have been clamoring for federal legislation. But no one has had solutions or concrete proposals to suggest and when our bill was tabled, it was often the same people who criticized it most strongly.
Faced with the innumerable comments on this bill, I feel somewhat like a referee between two fighters whom nothing can dissuade from doing everything to beat the other.
These two gladiators-a term I reluctantly use for extremists who tolerate no compromise-each have a share of public opinion behind them. Each has the support of 15 to 20 per cent of the population, but between them lies the majority, often called the "silent" majority, which certainly does not make the headlines.
One thing is for sure: No law will please everybody. If we want to protect the rights of the fetus, will we have to continue to take women to court? That is the terrible dilemma we are asked to resolve.
However, we cannot escape our responsibility, because what Canadians want now is an end to the confusion. They want the government to take a position and legislate in a way that strikes a fair balance between abortion on demand and criminalization. Such a law might not deal with the moral issues raised in this debate, but there will always be such problems which are hard to solve by legislation.
As my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, said, we were elected by the Canadian people to choose the course that will respect the rights of all concerned in as fair a way as possible.
That is why, Madam Speaker, I support this bill. However, I would like it to be just the starting point for another step. For all of us who care about respect for life, respect for the embiyo, the fetus, the unborn child, for all of us who deplore the alarming number of pregnancies that are terminated every year, it seems
urgent and imperative to me to lay the foundations for a real family policy.
The government's responsibility goes far beyond legislating or banning abortion. Since our role is to promote the welfare of the people, would it not be logical that, along with other government levels, with the private sector and with organizations dedicated to the future of our nation, we direct our combined efforts towards the prevention of abortion, prevention which in concrete terms means helping women who reject their pregnancy, and enhancing the desirability of the child and of the role of the mother?
AFEAS, a group well known for its enlightened and reasonable positions, advocates the establishment of family planning clinics for men and women alike where they would have access to services related to contraception, fertility, sterilization, and therapeutic abortion. A pregnant woman would be offered a full range of services such as reception, information, local resources reference and psycho-social support. A woman who does not want to have children should be aware of the many contraceptive methods which she and her mate can use.
On the other hand, it is just as important that a woman who wants to bear a child be in a position to look forward to maternity with enthusiasm and optimism. If this commendable aspiration is to be fulfilled, it is essential that a family policy have two objectives, one material, the other psychological.
In the first instance, the policy must eliminate or reduce as much as possible the destabilizing impact of pregnancy on the financial status of an individual, of a couple, or of a family. This could be done through tax measures which clearly favour women who want children. The baby bonus is a modest step in the right direction, but we have to think about the longer term. It is absolutely imperative that the career of family mother-or family father, in some cases-no longer be beyond the reach of most Canadians. The time has come for the tax burden to be distributed more equitably among those who are concerned about the survival of this nation and those who care only for their pleasure here and now.
As to the psychological objective of this policy, it seems to me to consist only in the enhancement of the contribution made by the father and mother. Even if we succeeded in making this contribution financially affordable, we would have achieve only half our goal if we did not make it socially worthwhile in the eyes of everyone. The mother who stays at home must be perceived as a

In our new society, the couple who decides freely to enrich their home with one or several children deserve the congragulations, encouragement, moral and financial support of the state. In short, they should get incentives to realize their objectives and to achieve their educative goal.
Personally, I think it is high time for the government to help society become more open to all life, as suggested last year by our Catholic Bishops. It should take society by the hand, walk side by side with it, educate it, convince it to help the family seek more children.
Thanks to such family human development assistance policies, abortion would practically disappear. Then and only then might we feel that we have done what we had to do to prevent abortion. That could be our most worthwhile contribution to the welfare of Canadian men and women.
